recommendations.text: Recommendations to the Dutch authorities 6.1.1. to increase the number of official veterinarians in the slaughterhouses to reach the permanent presence in accordance with article 9 of Directive 64/433/EEC as already recommended in the report on the veterinary mission to the Netherlands of 11 to 15 May 1998 (Doc XXIV/1399/98/final) 6.1.2. to introduce records for animal treatments on farms as quickly as possible 6.1.3. to issue detailed procedures for the official sampling by the end of March 1999 and inform the Commission hereof 6.1.4. to inform the Commission of the new structure of veterinary services as soon as plans are available 6.1.5. to include in such plans adequate training measures for inspectors charged with the sampling to guarantee a sampling strategy as laid down in Commission Decision 98/179/EC 6.1.6. to pursue the development of analytical methods for the detection of substances in the new product groups 6.1.7. to reconsider in the 1999 monitoring plan that the detection limits and levels of action for the examinations of Group A substances should be equal 6.1.8. to divide the responsibilities of the National Reference Laboratories for the specific substance groups before the 1 January 2001 6.1.9. to consider the assignment of the tasks of drawing up the monitoring plan, co-ordination of inspections, data collection and reporting to the Commission to one public body as required by article 4 of Council Directive 96/23/EC 12 of 13 RESIDUES ­ THE NETHERLANDS ­ OCT 98

Recommendations to the European Commission Services 6.2.1. to check the correction of deficiencies observed (levels of action, new methods, sampling procedures, responsibility for milk sampling) in the 1999 monitoring plan 6.2.2. to organize a follow-up mission on these items 13 of 13

Recommendations to the Commission services Consideration should be given to legal proceedings being taken against the Netherlands on the grounds that the veterinary presence as required by the Council Directive 71/118/EEC is not guaranteed in all slaughterhouses and cutting plants. The Commission should determine the general criteria for the special training for the staff of the undertaking in order to carry out operations provided in (a) and (b) of the second paragraph of point 47 of Chapter VIII of Annex 1, Council Directive 71/118/EEC, under the direct supervision of the official veterinarian, as foreseen in art. 8, third paragraph. The provisions of Annex C.II.3.B of Council Directive 93/119/EC on the protection of animals at the time of slaughter or killing, should be strengthened on grounds of logic and good practice.

Recommendations to the Member State The CA of the Netherlands should remedy without delay the deficiencies referred to under conclusions in Section 5 above. The rectification of the deficiencies in regard to the veterinary supervision of establishments (point 5.2.6) and veterinary supervision of slaughter hygiene and post-mortem inspection (point 5.2.7) are of special importance. In addition, they should clarify to the Commission why there is a difference between the instructions and legal requirements on the one side and the explanation and application of those requirements on the other hand concerning the veterinary supervision during transport (instruction No WWLZV012). Correction is recommended. The CCA of the Netherlands should within one month after reception of the final report inform the Commission of the actions either taken or planned to remedy the deficiencies identified and should indicate a clear timetable for all actions specified. In any event, unless there is adequate justification to the contrary, all actions to rectify deficiencies indicated in this report should be completed within 3 months of receipt of the final report. 23

To the Dutch veterinary authorities: The mission team recommends: 6.1.1. that the epidemiological enquiry be continued with all necessary intensity until the source of the original infection is identified. This would include a complete and precise picture of all the movements of the transport vehicles involved in the shipment of the two consignments to Spain during four weeks prior to the transport, and a complete report of the drivers. 6.1.2. that the Member States where the vehicles have been prior to and after the transport to Spain are informed about the exact routes of the vehicles.

To the Spanish veterinary authorities: The mission team recommends: 6.2.1. that detailed results of the post mortem examination of the six piglets taken from the two consignments originating from the Netherlands be provided. 6.2.2. that further information be provided on the identity of the three piglets from which virus was isolated. This would enable the Dutch CA to try to isolate virus from faeces collected in those pens of the farm of origin where these piglets were kept. 10 6.2.3. that further information be provided on any cleaning and disinfection of the truck and the trailer possibly carried out in Spain immediately after off-loading of the piglets.

To the European Commission: The mission team recommends: 6.3.1. that the Commission services study as a matter of urgency all aspects of cleaning and disinfection of all means of transport used for livestock with a view to issuing guidelines with European Union-wide application. The suitability of construction material used for means of transport should also be discussed. 11

To the Dutch Authorities The corrective measures already announced by the Dutch authorities during the final meeting regarding the inspection of fat suppliers to feeding manufacturers, the implementation of a monitoring programme for dioxins and PCBs in these companies, and the further supervision and reinforcement of restriction measures of suspect products should be carried out urgently and thoroughly. The suppliers of raw materials to the Suspect Belgian Company should be investigated by the responsible authorities, particularly with regard to the documentation accompanying consignments to that company. The supervision of all the relevant companies within the feed and food sector should be reinforced in the light of the experience acquired during the current dioxin problem. The current revision of the national legislative and policy framework related to the feed sector should be completed as a matter of priority and should incorporate the conclusions arising from the current dioxin problem. The Dutch authorities should inform urgently the Commission services about any relevant information on this matter. In addition, detailed writen information on the implementation of the corrective measures and further actions taken in the light of this report, should be made available to the Commission services within one month after the receipt of the final version of the report.

To the Commission Services The Commission services should consider reviewing the EU legal framework related to the use of recycled frying oils in feed production; 16 The Commission services should consider reviewing and reinforcing the legal framework concerning the traceability of raw materials used in feedingstuffs; The legislative measures put in place by the Dutch authorities regarding the implementation of Commission Decisions 1999/363/EC and 1999/368/EC should be further analysed. A general reflection on the potential conflicts between the confidentiality of private information obtained by laboratories and the general interest in the field of public health should be carried out in the appropriate fora. 17

To the competent authorities of The Netherlands: To provide a response, within one month of receipt of the translated final report, giving details of the actions, taken and planned, along with a timetable for completion of these actions to address: 8.1.1 the shortfall in staff and their training. 8.1.2 the other deficiencies referred to in this report (facilities, equipment, hygiene, documentation, registration, notification, veterinary checks, warehouses, transit and transhipments, updating national instructions, system for the inspection of BIPs, the implementation of Directive 97/78/EC and approvals for warehouses). In any event all deficiencies should be corrected within 3 months of receipt of the translated final report.

To the Commissions Services 8.2.1 to consider the transposition of Chapter 10, Annex I of Directive 92/118/EEC in Dutch law to determine whether, in relation to the storage of raw material for pet food, it is in line with EU-legislation.¦ 25/04/00 - 30032 16 DG (SANCO)/1205/1999 - MR Final 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/1205/1999 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report 8.1.1: Concerning the shortfalls in staff the Dutch Competent Authority has answered that it has begun to look at the number and quality of veterinary staff in relation to the amount of goods passing through the port of Rotterdam and Amsterdam airport. The plan to improve staffing levels is now being implemented and RVV has already recruited most of extra staff needed. An extensive training programme for the staff has been developed. 8.1.2: Concerning the other deficiencies the CA has described the actions planned to solve the shortcomings as follow: · Facilities, equipment and hygiene: will be improved at each site ( including warehouses and inspection centres ) · Documentation and registration: problems will be remedied shortly. The computerised system containing the results of inspections will shortly be updated. · Notification, preselection and identification: since 1 February 2000 weekly checks have been made to ascertain whether prior notification has been given for all veterinary products. Checks are carried out every two weeks to determine whether the products have been presented at an inspection post. · Veterinary checks: since 1 February 2000 the computerized system has been used to determine whether the frequency of physical checks on products is in line with the provision of Commission Decision 94/360/EC. In the view of the Dutch Government the seal checks carried out on a pilot basis are not in breach of the provisions in Commission Directive 97/78/EC and Commission Decision 92/525/EC. The Netherlands regard the area occupied by the port of Rotterdam as one inspection post. The procedure for laboratory testing has been amended as from 1 March 2000. · Warehouse: RVV will continue to make sure that warehouses/cold stores store only products for which they have been approved. The list of registered dealers who supply products to ships will be sent to the European Commission within the next three months. · Transit: from 1 April 2000 consignments of products leaving the EU via the BIP will be checked in accordance with Commission Decision 2000/208/EC. All transhipments have been registered since 1 November 1999. · Updating of national instructions: It is planned to amend the national instructions. 25/04/00 - 30032 17

recommendations.text: To further develop and advise farmers of ways of reducing the need to tail dock piglets.
To refine the parameters for assessing "appropriate lighting" in calf holdings.

To consider permitting a stockman, who can demonstrate the necessary knowledge and skill, to humanely kill animals such as moribund piglets. and to inform the Commission of the results of their efforts 6 months after receipt of the final report of this mission. 7.2. To the Commission Services 13 DG(SANCO) 1235/1999 MR final 7.2.1. Recommendations to the Commission services will be presented in a general report to be prepared after the completion of this series of mission to Member States. 8. COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO MISSION REPORT The Dutch authorities, in their comment of 4.1.2000 on the draft mission report, have suggested certain modifications of the text. Most of these modifications have been incorporated by the FVO into the final mission report. Dutch comments on point 7.1. of the mission report are expected at a later stage. 14
To consider clarifying if the storage of human consumption and not fit for human consumption products in the same rooms of an EC approved cold store is in accordance with EU legislation.

To consider the amendment of approval as following: -Eemshaven to extend the approval for NHC-T products (frozen only) if satisfactory guarantees are provided in relation to 6.5 hygiene and 6.3 facilities. -Eemshaven to limit the approval for HC-T products (frozen only) if no satisfactory guarantees are provided in relation to 6.5 hygiene and 6.3 facilities.

audits.title: Production of game (wild and farmed) and rabbit meal

recommendations.text: To take immediate measures to guarantee that game meat will not be placed on the market without health inspection. Written confirmation of the action taken must be sent to the Commission services within 3 working days after receiving the draft report.

To take immediate measures to guarantee that meat of wild boar will not be placed on the market without undergoing trichinae examination. Written confirmation of the action taken must be sent to the Commission services within 3 working days after receiving the draft report.

Within 3 months following the end of this mission, to carry out an investigation, in all the establishments approved for game meat, in relation to the non-compliance and deficiencies found. Written confirmation of the action planned must be sent to the Commission services within 3 working days after receiving the draft report. The result of this investigation must be sent to the Commission services after its completion.

Within 3 months following the end of this mission, to take measures to improve the veterinary supervision in the approved establishments, particularly the frequency of the visits, the health marking supervision, the required records of the results of the ante-mortem and post-mortem health inspection.

Within 3 months following the end of this mission, to inform the Commission services of the measures taken to ensure that the official veterinarians in charge of the approved establishments fulfil their duties in accordance with the EC requirements.

To ensure that the presence of the official veterinarians, in the approved establishments, is in compliance with EC requirements during ante-mortem and post-mortem health inspections and when meat is being worked on. 8.2. To the Commission Services 8.2.1 To consider whether further legal action should be taken against the Netherlands in light of the non-compliances found during this mission. 8.2.2 To carry out a follow up mission before the end of this year in order to assess the effectiveness of the action taken by the Dutch authorities in response to the recommendations of the Commission. 8.2.3 To provide a technical and a legal opinion in order to clarify whether 12 ­ It is possible to store the wild game more than 12 hours in the collection centre with the necessary equipment to chill the carcasses. ­ It is possible to have permanently derogated low capacity establishments for wild game marketing with a national health mark. 8.2.4 To provide a legal opinion on the requirements of the Council (Directive 92/45/EEC concerning the role of the official veterinarian in the supervision of the use of the commercial document which must accompany the wild game meat declared fit for human consumption (Article 3 (4) (iii)). 8.2.5 To establish a certificate model for the intra-Community trade of wild game in hide (Directive 92/45/EEC, Article 5 (3) (c)). Addendum to mission report DG(SANCO)/1062/2000 Competent authority response to the mission report In a letter dated 22 March 2000 the competent authorities stated that action had been taken immediately following the mission in relation to points 8.1.1, 8.1.2 and 8.1.3. In a further response, dated 4 April 2000, they confirmed the above actions and provided an action plan for improving the inspection of wild game as a response to recommendations 8.1.4, 8.1.5 and 8.1.6. 13

audits.title: Meat products, minced meat, meat preparations, casings

recommendations.text: To take action in order to rectify deficiencies seen in the casing plant visited.
To rectify deficiencies encountered in all the other plants visited and to ensure that similar deficiencies receive attention in all other plants in the Netherlands.
To ensure correct transposition of the EU provisions in regard to the approval of the establishments and the frequency of the microbiological checks in minced meat.
To ensure correct implementation of the frequency of microbiological checks in meat preparations.

To enhance veterinary supervision by the regional competent authority in order to monitor satisfactorily both the compliance of the establishments with EU requirements, and the proper implementation of the relevant legislation and working instructions by the local competent authority.

To strengthen veterinary supervision in regard to health marking. Information about the action taken in order to address the recommendation made in point 7.1.1 should be forwarded to the Commission within two months of the end of the mission. 22/12/00 - 24625 16 A plan describing the action to be taken to implement the recommendations made in points 7.1.2 to 7.1.6 should be provided to the Commission within three months of receiving the final report. This plan should include timetables for the completion of action required. 7.2 To the Commission Services 7.2.1 To consider developing Community guidelines for the performance of official controls in meat products and minced meat/meat preparations production. 7.2.2 To clarify the meaning of "sausage meat" as mentioned in Council Directive 94/65/EC, and define the health rules applicable to sausage meat as mentioned in Art.21 of the same Directive. 7.2.3 To clarify the acceptability under EC legislation of the irradiation of poultry meat, as permitted in the Dutch Commodity Act (Council Directives 99/2/EC and 99/3/EC). 7.2.4 In light of the Dutch authority response to point 7.1.3, to consider whether further action should be taken. 22/12/00 - 24625 17 ADDENDUM Competent authority response to mission report DG(SANCO)/1075/2000 The Dutch responded to the recommendations at points 7.1.1, 7.1.2, 7.1.5 and 7.1.6 indicating actions taken, or to be, taken and defining deadlines for the completion of some of those planned actions. The Dutch authority commented on the recommendations at points 7.1.3 and 7.1.4 with a view to demonstrating that the transposition and implementation of the provisions concerning the approval of certain establishments and the frequency of the microbiological checks in minced meat and meat preparations are in accordance to the relevant EU legislation. 22/12/00 - 24625 18
Continue the staff recruitment process to ensure that the RVV inspection service is fully staffed within the deadlines already established (mid 2001). Laboratory Service and Trichinella Controls

Supervision of sampling for trichinella should be improved to reduce the sampling error. Furthermore, the methodology used for trichinella testing in accredited and approved laboratories should be modified to conform to the specific requirements of the Annex to Council Directive 77/96/EEC. In the absence of any derogation from Community requirements (see 6.2) and in the light of an increase in trichinellosis in wild swine, all porcine animals for human consumption should be tested for trichinella. Further research is necessary to determine the reason for this increase in infection rate. Veterinary Supervision

Take steps to ensure that establishments are formally re-approved after major structural alteration or change in operation and ensure that all establishments in the NL have current documented approvals.

Ante mortem and post mortem inspection and training of auxiliaries to be conducted as described in Council Directive 64/433/EEC. In particular, all animals to be inspected ante-mortem by the OVS and the health marks (stamps and labels) to be applied correctly at all times.
Take steps to ensure that the establishment-based OVS has more input into the organisation and development of staff training programmes. Establishments

Deficiencies in the structure, layout, maintenance, cleanliness and operational hygiene encountered in the establishments visited (see chapter 5.8) should be rectified and similar deficiencies should receive attention in all other establishments. A report of the action taken, or to be taken and including a timetable for the correction of points 7.1.1 to 7.1.6 should be sent to the Commission Services within 3 months of the end of the mission. 20 7.2 To the Commission Services: 7.2.1 To consider whether the procedures used in the testing of samples for Trichinella Spiralis satisfy EC legislative requirements. 7.2.3 To consider whether the ante-mortem inspection procedures described in this report, and the initial response from the Dutch authorities, satisfy EC legislative requirements. If, in either case, it is considered that EC legislative requirements are not met, to consider whether further action should be taken. Addendum to Mission Report DG(SANCO)/1086/2000 The Dutch competent authorities commented on the draft report in a letter, dated 1 September 2000. The report has been reviewed in light of this response, and appropriate changes made, as indicated in the text of the final report. The authorities also provided initial details of their response to the recommendations made in this report. These will be followed up by the FVO in close co-operation with the national authorities. 21

audits.title: Plant protection product - Residues in foodstuffs of plant origin

recommendations.text: The competent authorities of the Netherlands should ensure that the control systems for residues work efficiently at all levels of the production chain [cf. chapter 6, indents (4) and (11)].

Monitoring for chlormequat on fresh pears and processed pear products (especially baby food) should be increased. Monitoring for chlormequat on carrots should be continued and also include processed products, especially baby food. The results should be notified to the Commission within the deadline set by the legislation [cf. chapter 6, indent (15)].

Inspections on illegal use of chlormequat in carrots should be continued and the results should be reported to the Commission in the annual report according to Art. 17 of Directive 91/414/EEC within the deadline set by the legislation.

The competent authorities should address all the other shortcomings listed in chapter 6, indents (1), (2), (6), (7), (12) and (16) in order to improve the control systems. A programme in response to chapter 8, indents (1) and (4) should be produced within a period of 6 months after receiving the final report. 8.2. To the Commission Services (1) The Commission Services should give guidance on how, in urgent cases, problems concerning the accreditation of laboratories could be solved. (2) The Commission Services should continue to support the Netherlands and the other Member States with a harmonised approach to risk assessment (acute and chronic), with regard to action to be taken in particular via the Rapid Alert System for Foodstuffs. 8.3. To all other Member States (1) All Member States should carefully monitor for chlormequat in pears and processed pear products and take appropriate action. 24 9. ADDENDUM Competent authority response to the recommendations in the report The competent authorities, in their comments, forwarded some details of actions, which have already been taken or will be taken to address the shortcomings listed in the mission report. They have set up a protocol for a better co-ordination between the different services involved in controls on marketing and uses and on residues of plant protection products. The inspectors of the AID got instructions with regard to the inspection procedures and check-lists to be carried on the spot. The problems of method validations for formulation and residue analysis have been partly addressed. Furthermore a procedure for emergency cases in the field of food safety has been established. However, the competent authorities expressed some reservations concerning the recommendation to increase monitoring for chlormequat on fresh pears and pear products. They consider it important to first analyse the recent monitoring data of the 2000 harvest in order to evaluate the necessity for further increase in monitoring activities. 25

Official Journal L 038 , 12/02/1998 p. 0010 - 0013 5 After the appearance of this particular problem, a substantial number of dairy farmers (7000, that is approximately 25 % of the Dutch dairy farmers) FODLPHG to have health problems on their farms. They claim to have suffered damages following the vaccination of their herds and to present their case, they created a foundation (SIS) which subsequently filed a claim for compensation against the vaccine producer for allegedly selling contaminated IBR vaccine. The claim is based on an inventory collated by SIS of the damages incurred by the industry.1 Conclusive links between these health problems and the vaccine have, however, not been established. The position of the CA so far, has been that these reports do not refer to a specific health problem, but primarily to socio-economic difficulties suffered by the farmers concerned and as such, the Dutch government has no direct involvement. The Commission services were informed by the Dutch authorities at an early stage of the existence of a contaminated batch of live attenuated vaccine for IBR and the consequences observed in treated animals. At a later stage, as press releases and parliamentary questions drew attention to the appearance of apparently high numbers of cattle in the Netherlands with a wasting condition, the Commission Services made a request to the MLNV for further clarification of the actual situation. Information was collected during interviews with the Dutch CA in relation to the development of this problem and the action they had taken. This is summarised below, and reflects information provided by these authorities during earlier communications with the Commission services. ­ The control of IBR started in 1998 in the Netherlands requiring the compulsory vaccination of all cattle, except for animals in officially IBR free herds. Both live and inactivated marker vaccines were available. In February 1999, after vaccination with live vaccine, severe symptoms of disease (leading to death in many instances) were recorded on 12 farms, one of them comprising separate production units. One batch of IBR vaccine was found to be contaminated with a virulent type of BVD virus (type 2). All cattle on these 12 farms, approximately 1400 animals, were slaughtered and destroyed. In order to obtain a better picture of the possible side effects of the vaccines, a record (the CA refers to an "inventory") was made of the symptoms observed after the IBR vaccination up to June 1999. Some of the symptoms reported related to cattle with a wasting condition (approximately 350 farms). These are cows in milk which over a period of time become emaciated. It is not clear whether or not these symptoms are connected to vaccination with IBR vaccines. Generally the condition of these animals improves if they are dried off. Tests have not yet revealed the presence of infectious agents. Every effort is being made to find the cause of the problem and in addition to tests on the affected animals, farm management is being looked into (high production holdings) as is the relation between the symptoms and the vaccine. Metabolic causes such as mineral deficiency are also being considered. 1 $ VXEVHTXHQW VWXG\ LGHQWLILHG IDUPV ZKHUH ORQJWHUP SUREOHPV ZHUH UHSRUWHG 12/07/00 - 38579 A number of animals appear to have shortages of cobalt/vitamin B12 and improve considerably when cobalt/vitamin B12 is administered. ­ The farms affected are being visited by the National Inspection Service for Livestock and Meat (RVV), an implementing body of the MLNV, and the Inspectorate for Health Protection, Commodities and Veterinary Public Health (IW&V) of the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (MVWS). If necessary the animals and/or products on these farms are declared unfit for human consumption. The Dutch authorities emphasise that, in their view there is no danger to public health from this problem. In the first place because no infectious agent, dangerous to humans, has been detected. In addition, the meat inspection system provides sufficient guarantees for public health. Furthermore they pointed out that the veterinary inspectors of the RVV work in accordance with the Meat Inspection Act and EU Directives. If disease is suspected, cattle are subjected to extensive tests. If during this investigation a disease is detected which renders the meat unfit for human consumption, the meat will be declared unfit. The meat will also be declared unfit if the veterinary inspector finds that the meat is abnormal, even though the type of disorder has not been diagnosed. The Dutch authorities had already assured the Commission services that the Dutch government has no doubt about the quality of milk and beef produced in the Netherlands. They also referred to the decision of the 1HWKHUODQGV Dairy Association (NZO), committing itself to exclude from the food chain all milk from identified problem herds ZLWK D YLHZ WR GLVSHOOLQJ SXEOLF XQHDVH This milk would be processed in such a way that it can be stored (i.e. milk-powder, butter) and would only be released for human consumption if conclusive laboratory results guarantee human health protection. In addition, the Dutch authorities had clarified that the NZO had commissioned the Animal Health Service (GD) to carry out an investigation into the veterinary problem on the farms concerned. The farm inspections will be carried out following a government-approved protocol. At the same time the authorities had declared that in spite of the media reports on this matter, which suggest a possible risk to public health, there is absolutely no reason to assume that this might be the case. They stated that milk produced by sick animals may not be sold for human consumption and is not accepted by dairy factories. Moreover, they stated that these factories run an extensive quality system that complies with Council Directive 92/46/EEC. Raw milk samples are thoroughly analysed in the laboratory. Raw milk is pasteurised and milk products undergo several checks in the factory before being shipped to retailers. According to this communication to the Commission, routine government checks have produced no evidence of any danger to public health. The authorities further stated that milk factories had not at any time indicated that the quality of milk concerned might in some way be compromised. recommendations.text: XEOLF VHUYLFHV DQG SULYDWH RUJDQLVDWLRQV LQYROYHG Two ministries are involved in control and surveillance: The MLNV, and in particular its YHWHULQDU\ policy department RI 9HWHULQDU\ )RRG 3ROLF\ DQG (QYLURQPHQWDO $IIDLUV (VVM), together with one of its implementing bodies, the RVV, are actively involved in the control and surveillance of problem herds. The MVWS, through its Inspectorate for Health Protection, Commodities and Veterinary Public Health (IW&V), is also involved. The main task of this Inspectorate is to enforce and control compliance with regulations on food, consumer articles and veterinary matters through the performance of supervision, detection and investigation activities. The AID is the implementing body of the MLNV that controls and investigates issues related to legislation that fall within the responsibility of the Ministry, as well as general criminal law. Some duties that fall under the responsibility of the MVWS, such as the control of animal disease prevention and eradication aspects of the Meat Inspection Act, are also covered by the AID. At this stage, this service, has not been involved since no legal irregularities have been detected. The animal health services (GD), a private body at the service of the primary agricultural sector, performs many tasks for the Product Boards as well as for the Government. The GD mainly concentrates on the surveillance and diagnosis of animal diseases. It has been given the task by the NZO of carrying out an investigation on the farms identified as having a problem - following guidelines set up by the MLNV DQG 09:6, but has also been involved in the complaint actions set up by the LTO (see next paragraph). The GD operates with inspectors and three diagnostic laboratories, which perform routine analysis on the most common non- notifiable livestock diseases. The service generally contacts ID-Lelystad if further research is required. There is a legal obligation for the GD to inform the RVV of QRWLILDEOH GLVHDVH problems in herds. The national reference laboratory for the diagnosis of OIE list A and other notifiable animal diseases is ID-Lelystad. This laboratory was directly dependent on the MLNV until it was JUDQWHG VHPL DXWRQRPRXV VWDWXV in 1999. INTRODUCTION The mission to the Netherlands was the fifth of a series of inspections to all Member States to audit the plant health system in the potato sector. A pre-mission questionnaire was sent to the Dutch plant protection authorities in advance of the mission. The answers to this questionnaire provided an overview of the Dutch plant health system in the potato sector and of the general health status of the potato production in the Netherlands.

MISSION DETAILS The mission in the Netherlands took place from 3 to 7 July 2000. The mission team comprised 2 inspectors from the Food and Veterinary Office (FVO), and 2 Member State experts. Representatives from the Dutch plant protection service accompanied the inspection team during the whole mission. An opening meeting was held on 3 July 2000 in Wageningen with the central competent authority. At this meeting, the objectives of, and itinerary for, the mission were confirmed by the inspection team. A closing meeting with the central competent authority was held in Wageningen on 7 July 2000. The following sites were visited: COMPETENT AUTHORITY VISITS Competent authority Central 2 Regional 2 LABORATORY VISITS Official laboratories 3 Private laboratories 3 PLANT HEALTH CONTROL SITES Potato breeding/multiplication stations 2 Potato producers 6 Potato packing/despatch stations 2 Potato processing plants 1

OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objectives of the mission were to assess (1) the performance of the various bodies involved in the national plant health system with reference to the potato sector, and (2) the implementation of the relevant EU legislation in this area. 1

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the provisions of Article 19a of Council Directive 77/93/EEC1, last amended by Commission Directive 1999/53/EC2. The legislation (in addition to Council Directive 77/93/EEC) of particular relevance for this mission, was: ­ Council Directive 69/464/EEC3 on the control of potato wart disease, ­ Council Directive 69/465/EEC4 on the control of potato cyst eelworm, ­ Council Directive 93/85/EEC5 on the control of potato ring rot, ­ Council Directive 98/57/EC6 on the control of potato brown rot, ­ Commission Directive 93/50/EEC7 on the registration of producers, warehouses and dispatching centres.

recommendations.text: BACKGROUND Regarding statistical data in this and following chapters: If no reference is given in the text, the figures were provided by the Dutch authorities in the pre-mission questionnaire or during the mission. 5.1. Previous missions to the Netherlands concerning potatoes During the last five years, the Food and Veterinary Office of the European Commission (FVO) has carried out 4 missions to the Netherlands with relevance to potatoes. All 4 missions focused solely on brown rot (caused by Ralstonia solanacearum) and the subsequent implementation of the Commission Decision on temporary additional measures as regards the Netherlands to prevent the spread of the disease. (Commission Decision 95/506/EC8 as last amended by Commission Decision 98/738/EC9). During these missions, the Netherlands was generally found to be complying with the requirements. 1 OJ No. L 26, 31.1.1977, p. 20 2 OJ No. L 142, 5.6.1999, p. 29 3 OJ No. L 323, 24.12.1969, p. 1 4 OJ No. L 323, 24.12.1969, p. 3 5 OJ No. L 259, 18.10.1993, p. 1 6 OJ No. L 235, 21.8.1998, p. 1 7 OJ No. L 205, 17.8.1993, p. 22 8 OJ No. L 291, 6.12.1995, p. 48 9 OJ No. L 354, 30.12.1998, p. 62 2 5.2. Potato production in the Netherlands In 1998, potato production represented 3.7% of the Netherlands 's gross agricultural output and 7.3% of the gross output in crop production (EUROSTAT). The Netherlands is the second largest producer of potatoes in the EU. Over the last three years, about 180,000ha per year, equivalent to 20-25% of the total cropping area, were grown with potatoes. Yields are generally high; thus, in 1999 a total of 8.2 million tons was produced which means a national average of about 45t/ha. The Netherlands is the EU's largest producer of seed potatoes. Over the last three years, almost 40,000ha of certified seed potatoes were grown per year. 5.3. Potato trade in the Netherlands Seed potatoes The Netherlands has, as an average over the last five years, imported about 19,000t of seed potatoes per year, mainly from Belgium, France and United Kingdom (EUROSTAT). The Netherlands is the largest exporter of seed potatoes in the world. On average over the last five years, 600,000t were exported per year; about 60% to other Member States and 40% to Third Countries (EUROSTAT). Other potatoes The Netherlands is a large importer of potatoes for processing (mainly for chips) and for starch production. Of the 1999 harvest, 1.2 million t were imported, of which 600,000 were for processing, 400,000 for starch production and 200,000 for direct consumption. On average over the last five years, the Netherlands has exported about 900,000 tons per year of ware/industrial potatoes, of which over half went to Germany and Belgium (EUROSTAT). In addition, processed products equivalent to 2-3 million tons of fresh potatoes are exported each year.

MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. Plant health system in the Netherlands 6.1.1. Structure of the plant health system The Plant Health Service (Plantenziektenkundige Dienst = PD) has been designated as the "single and central authority" for plant health as understood in Article 1 (6) of Council Directive 77/93/EEC. The PD is an 3 implementing agency of the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature Management and Fisheries (MANMF), directly under the responsibility of the Minister. The MANMF has the responsibility for plant health legislation and represents the Netherlands at the international level (e.g. the EU Council meetings, FAO, IPPC, Third Countries). The PD deals with technical questions related to plant health and represents the Netherlands in the EU Standing Committee on Plant Health. The PD carries out or supervises all activities related to plant health. Three accredited private institutions cooperate with the PD in potato plant health. The Netherlands General Inspection Service for Agricultural Seed and Seed Potatoes (Nederlandse Algemeine Keuringsdienst = NAK), a private foundation that co-operates closely with the PD, is by far the most important of these institutions. It is in charge of the certification of seed potatoes including the issuing of plant passports. With regards to quarantine organisms, the NAK carries out a substantial share of the screening tests for R. solanacearum and the majority of the laboratory analyses of soil samples for potato cyst nematodes. The two other institutions are private laboratories that are accredited for the soil sampling and analysis for potato cyst nematodes. They do not have any other function in potato plant health. In addition, a third laboratory is in the process of being accredited. 6.1.2. Human and financial resources Human resources In total, the PD headquarters employs around 150 staff (including laboratory personnel). In the 12 district offices, there is about 200 staff. PD management estimates that about 80% of the PD field inspections and laboratory tests are done on potatoes while more than 50% of the total PD resources are dedicated to the potato sector. The NAK has 280 employees, of whom 110 are field staff involved in potato field and seed lot inspection. The NAK estimates that about 45% of its turnover comes from potato inspection and certification. Four years of successful studies at a middle level agricultural school is the minimum educational requirement for plant health inspectors, both at the PD and at the NAK. PD inspectors have access to technical training. NAK inspectors meet once a year for an instruction session. When necessary, the PD organises specific additional training sessions for NAK staff (as e.g. when brown rot occurred). Senior staff at the PD headquarters is entitled to participate in management training courses, which are offered by external institutions. 4 Financial resources The PD is partly funded through the government budget and partly through fees that are charged for inspections and laboratory analyses. The resources are allocated on the basis of an annual work programme, which is prepared by the PD and approved by the MANMF. In the event of an emergency, additional funding can be obtained. The private institutions cooperating with the PD in plant health are funded through cost covering fees paid by the agricultural producers. They do not receive any financial support through the government budget. 6.1.3. Internal or external assessment of the institution's work The MANMF drafts annual strategic work plans in consultation with the PD. The PD then works out detailed task oriented work plans. Due to its agency status, the PD is required to keep the Ministry informed about its activities on a regular basis. Every three months, a review of the work progress and the financial status takes place, in which the director of the PD reports to the management board of MANMF. The NAK has its own quality management system. In addition, the NAK is audited by the PD at least three times a year. The PD produces a report of each audit. 6.1.4. Transposition and enforcement of legislation The transposition of EU Directives related to plant health is done by MANMF in close collaboration with the PD, which provides technical input. Three types of legislation may be used to transpose EU legislation: laws such as the crop protection act, royal decrees, and regulations. Laws must pass parliament and are only used for fundamental changes in the plant health legislation. Royal decrees must be approved by the cabinet, while regulations can be made by the MANMF alone. All directives of relevance for plant quarantine in potatoes have been transposed in the Netherlands. The General Inspection Service (Algemene Inspectie Dienst = AID), which operates under the Minister of Agriculture, is the leading institution with regard to law enforcement in the agricultural sector. Most irregularities in the implementation of plant health legislation are detected by the PD or the NAK, which then pass on the cases to the AID. The AID carries out the formal investigation on the basis of which, a prosecutor decides on corrective measures. The implementation of corrective measures is verified by AID. 5 6.1.5. Contingency plans PD inspectors have a handbook on quarantine organisms. It contains instructions on how to handle brown rot and ring rot outbreaks and details on the sampling procedures within the respective monitoring programmes. 6.2. Seed potatoes in the Netherlands 6.2.1. Potato breeding and seed certification Breeding A gene bank for wild Solanum species and original South American cultivars is held by the Centre for Genetic Resources, within Wageningen University and Research Centre. The collection contains about 1950 accessions of 120 wild species and 750 accessions of 5 primitive species. Cultivated potato varieties are held by breeders. The potato breeding system in the Netherlands is to a large extent based on a system of numerous part or full time "associated breeders" that receive the original clones from a breeding company and then carry out the selection work. The inspection team visited such a company whose varieties constitute 35% of the Dutch seed market. This company handles 140,000 clones per year of which 100,000 are dealt with at its 75 associated breeders. Thus, of the company's variety list, over 95% come from its associated breeders. The company is involved during various stages in the selection process, e.g. for assessing qualities like processing properties or pest resistance that cannot easily be evaluated in the field with traditional methods. Multiplication and production of seed The majority of pre-basic seed still comes from traditional clonal selection done at 600-700 specialised seed farms. However, the use of tissue culture propagation is increasing and is now the basis for about 40% of the pre-basic seed. The material enters at the farm level as minitubers, mainly produced in the Netherlands where there are 7 such producers. The NAK is the largest of these with about half of the total production. The figure below outlines the certification system in the Netherlands. The higher grades of seeds are primarily produced in the northern areas. Certified seed is also grown in the western and central parts of the country. In total there are over 2,600 seed farms in the Netherlands, of which one third grow less than 5ha. 6 The certification is, as mentioned before, done by the NAK. A database has been developed that contains information on all the lots certified or in the process of certification. Data are immediately available for the last four growing seasons. The PD has reading access to this database, which facilitates trace back and forward when quarantine diseases are detected in the seed production. For production and use of farm saved seed, see 6.3.1 below. 6.2.2. Plant health in the breeding and multiplication of seeds 6.2.2.1. Non quarantine pests With regard to the breeding for resistance, Phytophthora infestans (late blight) and Erwinia carotovora (blackleg) have the highest priority of the non-quarantine diseases. In the first stages of the multiplication chain, viruses and other agents are avoided, as mentioned before, mainly by traditional clonal selection of healthy plants and only partly by use of meristem culture techniques. The higher grades of seed potatoes are furthermore grown in coastal areas with low risk of aphid transmission of viruses. 6.2.2.2. Quarantine pests in the breeding material Import permits for material from Third Countries for breeding or scientific purposes are issued on the basis of a written application and if the importer is not well known by the PD, a filled in questionnaire and possible inspection visit to the importer's premises. The material is placed in quarantine either at the PD or, if multiplication is needed to have enough material for the testing, at the NAK. Testing for quarantine potato viruses and viroids is performed on all imports from outside the EU and on all material taken out of the gene bank, if such testing has not been done before. In addition, at least 60 accessions per year from the gene bank are tested as they are being multiplied for maintenance, with the goal of eventually having the whole gene bank tested. In total, around 200 potato accessions are tested each 7 year. The below table gives an overview over the number of interceptions in the period of 1989 to 1997: Number of interceptions in the post-entry quarantine testing 1989 to 1997 Virus Andean potato latent virus Andean potato mottle virus Potato black ringspot virus Potato leafroll virus Potato spindle tuber viroid Potato virus A Potato virus M Potato virus S Potato virus T Potato virus V Potato virus X Potato virus Y Potato yellowing virus 1989 1 10 4 13 12 31 - - 1 17 - 1990 1991 5 8 1 10 16 - - 4 5 - 1992 1993 1 1 2 10 - - 5 3 - 1994 1995 61 2 24 - - 1 2 - 1996 1997 1 3 9 9 26 - - 17 20 - 37 2 - - 3 4 - 3 2 16 - - 1 24 - 1 23 7 2 1 In addition to the virus testing, the above material is also tested for ring rot (caused by Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus) and brown rot. During the breeding process, at least at the visited breeding station mentioned in 6.2.1 above, each generation of the material is sampled and tested for both ring rot and brown rot. In general, all potential varieties entering the breeding companies'trials and the official selection are tested for brown rot. After the official selection, all potential varieties are tested for both brown rot and ring rot. 6.2.2.3. Quarantine pests in the multiplication of seed potatoes Brown rot and ring rot Pre-basic material: In the clonal selection system, brown rot testing is done systematically from the third generation of pre-basic seed and in each generation thereafter (there can be up to five generations of pre-basic seed ­ see figure above). Systematic testing for ring rot is done in the third stage only. The minitubers from the tissue culture propagation system enter the regular multiplication scheme as first year clones and are from then subject to the same testing for brown rot and ring rot. In addition, all Dutch initial stock for tissue culture propagation is tested for both brown rot and ring rot. Basic and certified seed: All lots of basic and certified seed are systematically tested for brown rot with at least one sample per 25t. Thus, over the various basic and certified seed grades of the 1999 harvest, a 8 total of 62,452 samples were tested for brown rot. With a total seed potato area of 39,200ha this averages one sample per 0.6ha. As the brown rot testing is obligatory for all seed lots and as such is a part of the certification process, the producers are charged for this testing. For ring rot, surveys are carried out aimed at testing around 10% of the seed lots each year, including all farms that grow grade elite. The selection of seed farms and lots to be tested for ring rot is done centrally by the PD using the NAK database on seed producers. Thus, of the 1999 harvest, 3,806 samples of basic and certified seed were tested in this general survey, giving an average sample density of one sample per 10.3ha. The ring rot tests are paid by the PD. Farm saved seed: Samples are also taken from farm saved seed, produced on the starch potato farms. Thus of the 1999 harvest of about 4,600ha of such farm saved seed, 4,445 samples were tested for brown rot and 952 for ring rot. This is included in the figures in the below tables. Visual inspections (in 1999, around 500) are also carried out. Of all the above samples, 62 (of which 13 came from farm saved seed) tested positive for brown rot. During the field inspections of farm saved seed, 3 cases with visual symptoms were found. Some of the positive samples mentioned came from the same lots, and in total 26 lots were found infected. Some of these lots were again clonally related so that the infections found can be grouped into 14 unrelated "cases" involving 9 varieties: Diamant, Kardal, Bintje, Elkana, Kartel, Desiree, Karakter, Karnico and Seresta. The year before, i.e. 1998 harvest, only two10 samples from certified seed potatoes and three10 from farm saved seed were positive. From the 1997 harvest, 30 samples were found positive. While in the 1998 harvest there was one case of ring rot in seed potatoes, for which the origin could not be determined, all seed samples tested for ring rot of the 1999 harvest were found negative. In addition to the above sampling during the certification process, samples are also taken in exports in response to importing Third Countries' specific requirements. Thus of the 1999 harvest, 1,951 such samples were tested for brown rot and 691 for ring rot. All these samples were negative for both diseases. Recommendations on epidemio-surveillance of BSE · The competent authorities should study carefully the potential BSE suspects, which were ruled out by the BSE expert teams. If necessary they should try to find a solution for these animals which did not recover completely or where an alternative diagnosis could not be clearly established at the time when they were examined by the BSE expert team (e.g. a longer observation period or the obligation to sample these animals should they die or be slaughtered). · Should cattle brain samples from the Animal Health Service continue to be examined for BSE, they should be accompanied with more comprehensive information, and a more targeted approach for their selection should be used.

Recommendations for the active surveillance program · In order to be able to establish the age of cattle to be sampled in the rendering plant an online access to the central bovine database in the sampling area should be provided. · Provisions should be established to ensure that all cattle collected by the rendering plant are identifiable. · It should be considered to collect and transport fallen cattle in vehicles separate from other SRM. · In order to be able to sample the relevant animals in the emergency slaughterhouses it has to be ensured that the age of the animals can be established.

Recommendations on Specified Risk Materials · The competent authorities should issue clear instructions: for the slaughterhouse staff removing Specified Risk Material, aimed at avoiding contamination of carcasses with Specified Risk Material, and as regards workers' protection, Aimed at enabling reconciliation, in particular the keeping of records, and taking due account of the necessary co-operation of the services involved, and monitor these activities. · Procedures should be issued to ensure that the age of cattle to be slaughtered is established before slaughter in order to guarantee that Specified Risk Material is removed from cattle from one year of age. 22

Recommendations on the feed ban · Although the use of meat and bone meal for the production of feed for farmed animals is forbidden since 1 January 2001, controls should still continue including raw materials. 23 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 1303/2000 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Dutch authorities stated in their comments that: Fallen stock without ear tags are not collected by the rendering plant anymore. If such cattle are presented for collection the General Inspection Service is informed which will then investigate. Moreover, officials taking samples from fallen stock in the rendering plant since March 2001 have on-line access to the central database enabling them to check the age of cattle. Since March 2001 all fallen cattle over 30 months of age are sampled and tested for BSE. An online access to the central bovine database in the sampling area of the rendering plant has been established. Fallen stock is nowadays collected separately from other Specified Risk Materials. Slaughterhouses are now obliged to supply a list with cattle identification data (e.g. the age of the animals to be slaughtered) before slaughter and officials have to check the identification of 10 % of the animals every day. An instruction was issued end of January 2001 laying down rules for monitoring of the collection of Specified Risk Materials, identification, storage, refrigeration, staining and removal of Specified Risk Materials. In this context it is also stated that the quality of removal of Specified Risk Materials is the industries responsibility. Since the end of March 2001, slaughterhouses and cutting plants are obliged to weigh Specified Risk Materials and keep records of these data before collection by the rendering plant. Instructions on removal and reconciliation of Specified Risk Material have been issued. According to the sampling plan for 2001 more than 2400 samples from compound feed and raw materials were planned to be taken. However, due to the Foot and Mouth Disease outbreak this figure will most probably not be fulfilled. 24

Recommendations on the epidemio-surveillance of BSE - The Dutch authorities should consider a more formal and documented monitoring system of control by the central and regional level on the performance of the active and passive surveillance at the local level; - The Dutch authorities must install an official procedure in the slaughterhouse to ensure that no parts of examined animals bearing the health mark can leave the slaughterhouse until a negative result to the rapid test has been obtained;

Recommendations on the feed ban 8.1.3. - The Dutch authorities have to take immediate action to install a channelling system for derogated PAP. - The Dutch authorities should consider shortening the delay for receiving the results in the actual control programme of the feed ban. - The Dutch authorities should consider a proper risk assessment when elaborating the control programme of the feed ban. Recommendations on Specific Risk Materials - The Dutch authorities should evaluate the performance of the proper staining at regular intervals; 30 8.1.4. - The Dutch authorities should take immediate actions to ensure 8.1.5. correct channelling of SRM to final incineration. The CCA should take measures to put a uniform documented system in place to enable reconciliation at every stage of the chain and monitored at regular intervals. Recommendations regarding tallow - The Dutch authorities should improve the awareness and strengthen the official control on the purification of ruminant fat used in feed for ruminants. Recommendations regarding the establishments - The Dutch authorities should take immediate action to correct the deficiencies noted in the establishments visited and re- assess other similar establishments in the Netherlands to review if the same deficiencies exist. - The Dutch authorities should take immediate action to prevent that meat destined for the local market is put into intra community trade. The Dutch authorities should inform the Commission Services of the follow up actions taken to resolve the problems referred to in point 8.1.2, first indent, point 8.1.3, second indent and point 8.1.4. within one month of the receipt of the translated draft report. A plan concerning the actions to be taken regarding the implementation of the other points referred to in recommendations 8.1.1. ­ 8.1.5 should be provided to the Commission within one month of the receipt of the translated final report. This plan should include timetables for the specific actions required. 31 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 3305/2001 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Dutch authorities announced in their written comments of 25 January 2002 that they had taken the following actions in relation to the recommendations: · Internal checks and audits are being carried out by the RVV-Centraal`s department for quality management on the performance at the local level of the teams involved in the sampling activities covered by the active surveillance programme. · By reviewing official instructions the Dutch authorities have installed a channelling system for derogated PAP. · As from 1 January 2002 the delay of receiving the results in the control programme of the feed ban has been reduced to ten days. · The performance of the proper staining of SRM is included in the action programme "intensification of SRM checks/handling" by the Dutch authorities. · To ensure correct channelling of SRM and enable reconciliation at every stage of the chain the Dutch authorities have amended the transport document for the SRM to the rendering plant. · In order to improve awareness and strengthen the official control on the purification of tallow an instruction has been circulated by the Dutch authorities. · Immediate action to correct the detected deficiencies in the establishments visited has been taken. However, as regards certain recommendations, the Dutch authorities expressed some reservations: · The Dutch authorities consider a company procedure approved by the Competent Authority as equivalent to an official procedure to ensure that parts of the slaughtered animals do not leave the slaughterhouse until a negative result of the rapid test is available. · The Dutch authorities do not consider a formal risk assessment as necessary in elaborating the control programme of the feed ban taking into account the separation of the production of ruminant feed and other agricultural feed. 32
Urgent steps should be taken to identify and register small holdings, so that a complete picture of the animal population is established.

To carry out frequent checks on the data already available to ascertain whether significant discrepancies exist between the numbers and identities of animals recorded as present on farms in the animal movement database, the numbers and identities of animals vaccinated and the numbers and identities of those subsequently culled. If discrepancies are detected, the present methods for collection and checking of data should be revised.

To ensure the prompt destruction of all part-used bottles of vaccine. 9.2. To the Commission Services To monitor closely the development of the situation in The Netherlands particularly in regard to culling of vaccinated animals. 13 In their response to the draft report, the Dutch authorities commented that the culling of animals in the 2km vaccination zones outside the Noord Veluwe vaccination zone has begun and that it has now also been decided to cull the cattle as well. 21 To study the response of the Dutch authorities to the FMD outbreaks with the view to disseminating the lessons learned to other Member States. ADDENDUM Competent authority response to the recommendations in the report As part of their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities have provided a chronological survey of national regulations introduced between 23 February and 6 April 2001 in connection with the outbreaks of FMD. audits.title: Implementation of Council Directive 91-493-EEC (fishery products) and of Council Directive 91-492-EEC (bivalve molluscs)

recommendations.text: Legislation The Commission services should be provided with information on the amendment (to the current Dutch legislation) in respect to the registration of wholesale markets and fishing vessels.

Competent Authority The RVV, being the competent authority, should be effectively empowered to enforce the suspension of the production of establishments, whenever the situation calls for a potential public health risk and/or when major deficiencies are repetitively demonstrated.

Laboratories The necessary actions should be undertaken to rectify the deficiencies noted in relation to the testing methods in the different laboratories visited during the mission. The RIVM should strengthen its co-ordination activities regarding the use of the rat bio-assay in the laboratory responsible for performing analyses on the monitoring of marine biotoxins. 24 As a general remark and in accordance with RVV instructions all laboratories carrying out activities related to the fishery products and bivalve molluscs sectors should be accredited. Approval by the RVV of external laboratories involved in performing analyses linked to the own-checks of the companies should be established as a routine. The NRL for bacteriological and viral contamination in bivalve molluscs should be officially appointed without further delay.

Official controls In general, the official controls should be more targeted in the areas of inspection visits and the follow up actions strengthened in the premises. This should also include random official sampling, at establishments' level, to verify and confirm the reliability of the analyses performed by the companies in the framework of their "own-checks" plans.

Monitoring programme on bivalve molluscs The RVV should organise a system of supervision of the PV as regards the activities linked to the bivalve molluscs sector. The RVV should also establish a formal protocol regarding the procedures of laboratories performing analyses linked to monitoring programmes on bivalve molluscs, in particular for bacteriological and biotoxins determination. Written evidence of these interrelations should be recorded. It is recommended that the number of sampling points for the routine monitoring on biotoxins/phytoplankton and microbiological aspects in the re-watering plots should be increased. The laboratory methods for microbiological and biotoxins analyses should be those laid down in the relevant EU legislation and recommended by the Community Reference Laboratories (CRLs). The samples for phytoplankton analyses should be taken using an integrated method to ensure that the total water column is sampled. A tube sample or a vertical net haul should be used, especially in areas where the water stratifies.

Sites visited The deficiencies observed by the inspection team in the plants visited should be rectified; in particular the traceability of products and the correct use of the official health mark should be strictly supervised during official inspections. If found, similar deficiencies in other approved plants should be rectified in accordance with the requirements of the relevant EU legislation.

Written guarantees Written guarantees should be forwarded to the Commission services in respect of all the points listed above within 25 working days after receipt of the translated version of the draft report, including an action plan in which a detailed timetable for all the necessary corrective actions is drawn up. 25 Moreover, the Commission services would expect to receive from the RVV, within the same above-mentioned deadline, evidence of the implemented measures in relation to the following points: - the supervision on the correct use of the official health mark; - the follow-up actions undertaken by inspectors during the official controls, as regards outstanding deficiencies in the establishments as well as a programme for random official sampling at processing establishments level; - the revision of the frequency and geographical distribution of sampling in the so called "re-watering plots"; - the discrepancies with the EU relevant legislation on laboratory methods used for certain analyses in the bivalve molluscs sector; - the role of the NRL as regards the supervisory activity on the laboratories performing biotoxins analyses. 26

recommendations.text: Live bivalve molluscs a. The official (and own-check) analyses should be carried out according to the methods provided by the relevant Community legislation (Council Directive 91/492/EEC and Decision 2002/225/EC), and recommended by the Community Reference Laboratories (CRLs). Any other method should be validated against the European reference methods. b. Once the mandatory method for the monitoring of faecal coliform contamination is adopted, the Dutch CA and the operators should reassess the effectiveness of the purification process in use by resorting to adequate sampling points and methods. c. The interpretation of the microbiological results for the production area classification should be revised in order to comply with the relevant provision of Directive 91/492/EEC, in particular once the mandatory method for the monitoring of faecal coliform contamination is adopted. d. The RIVM should strengthen its co-ordination activities as NRL for bacteriological and viral contamination in bivalve molluscs. e. Official sampling for laboratory testing of end-products (LBM) regarding biotoxins should be carried out.

Fishery products a. Official controls should be more targeted on specific and actual problems, i.e. histamine in tuna, Listeria monocytogenes in smoked products at production level and/or distribution centres. This should also include random official sampling to verify and confirm the reliability of the analyses performed by the establishments in the framework of their "own-check" plans and to cover additional aspects of interest like contaminants or correct determination of best before dates. b.
