The method equivalent to the MPN method will be used for the classification of production areas. Classification will be based on 5 samples and will be interpreted as proposed in the new draft Regulation on microbiological criteria. This method is current practice in the Netherlands. d. RIVM will bring their activities in line with the legislation. e. Testing on molluscs imported from other production areas than those in the Netherlands will be intensified. 5.2 Fishery products a. A programme is foreseen for testing extra samples on histamine and Listeria, although previous years' results do not suggest that products in the Netherlands are exceeding the standards. However, attention will be paid to the reliability of the own-check analysis results. 05/07/05 - 36080
The competent authorities should transpose and implement Directive 1999/45/EC on classification, packaging and labelling of dangerous preparations.

The competent authorities should ensure that Maximum Residue Levels are established for all active substances at the time of first 27 authorisation of the substances, in accordance with Article 4.1 (f) of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authorities should ensure that measurement uncertainty of residue analytical methods is estimated following the provisions of Guidance document on Quality Control procedures for pesticides analysis (Doc. SANCO/10476/2003).

The competent authorities should carry out the validation of the analytical method applied in case of high fat content matrixes as required by the Guidance document on residue analytical methods (Doc. SANCO/825/2000).

The competent authorities should consider prioritising the control on use and marketing of PPPs regionally, on the basis of hazards evaluation linked to regional agricultural productions and marketing of PPPs.
The competent authorities should ensure that all results of the control activities on marketing and use are reported to the Commission according to Art.17 of Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authorities should ensure that the results of the national monitoring plan on pesticide residues are notified completely to the Commission according to the guidance issued annually (DOC SANCO 4/2004). These results should include all information on analyses for chlormequat residues.

The competent authorities should consider all the other shortcomings listed in chapter 6.1, in particular indents (9), (10), (16) and (24) in order to improve effectiveness of the control systems. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation.

ADDENDUM In their response to the draft report, the Dutch authorities stated, in relation to Recommendation (5) that " the prioritisation of the control on use and marketing of PPPs regionally on the basis of hazard evaluation has already been done. In addition, three inspectorates draw up regional control plans relating to the inspection of regional or local production and the associated problems. The initiative for this is with the inspectorates. The plan, reasons and results are communicated to head office and the other AID inspectorates." 28 In relation to Recommendation (3), the Dutch authorities consider that "the use of a measurement uncertainty of 50% is not at odds with document SANCO/10476/2003, given that this value is estimated on the basis of proficiency tests, as discussed in paragraph 85 of this document." In relation to Recommendation (4), the Dutch authorities consider that " the scope of Directives 90/642/EU and 86/362/EU barely extends to products with a high fat content. Neither do they arise in the several-year coordinated monitoring programme, which means that they have low priority in the VWA (Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority) validation process. Document SANCO/825/2000 applies to applicants for registration who develop a method for monitoring and enforcement (after registration) and is a useful source of information for control laboratories. It is certainly the case that a performance check that stops short of full validation should be enough for the implementation of a method already validated by the applicant in another laboratory." Finally in relation to Recommendation (7) the Dutch authorities consider that "in accordance with the reporting guidelines, the Netherlands has, for a number of years now, been reporting in good time to the Commission. Unfortunately, some analyses for chlormequat, where no residue was found, were not included in 2002. In general, it is not necessary to report on the methods used on a particular sample. The Netherlands has proposed in the residue work group that a separate reporting sheet be included for this." 29

Application of ABP requirements along the chain The ABP requirements are largely applied as described by the CCA. However, some shortcomings were noted: Observations: 9 A frequent finding was the lack of compliance with provisions on labelling and commercial documentation that accompanies category 3 ABP and products therefrom. This applied to many consignments coming from other Member States and frequently for consignments sent from Dutch establishments. Sometimes, no indication was included as regards category of the materials, particularly when the material was an ABP produced from raw material fit for human consumption. Approval numbers for sender and customer were also frequently lacking. Understanding of the need for categorise the material as ABP once its intended use had been decided was not totally clear to all operators in the ABP chain and all official inspectors met. 12 9 In one fat processing plant still approved under previous legislation collecting only category 3 material, deficiencies were noted as regards categorisation of incoming materials with no indication of their category or species of origin. Commercial documents had been stamped with these details at arrival by this plant of destination. Category 3 rendered fats were sent normally to feed establishments and petfood plants. However, two of the customers acting as intermediaries for ABP were plants approved under foodstuffs legislation that had not been approved as intermediaries in the ABP chain (15). 9 In one intermediate plant for category 3 material RVV staff advised the mission team that only 50% of the ANIMO messages sent to Germany accompanying consignments of MBM were being acknowledged at arrival. 9 In a plant approved for processing manure the mission team noted that the operator had recently discontinued the notification to the CA for preparation of ANIMO messages that must accompany consignments of processed manure to other Member States. Allegedly, the reason was the high administrative burden that this placed on their daily operation. In addition, unprocessed dried manure was sent also to other Member States, mainly Germany, always accompanied by a health certificate as agreed beforehand with the CCA of the country of destination. 9 An establishment visited and approved as a technical plant for wool was acting as an intermediary and the mission team noted that raw material was coming from several cattle dealers and farmers. In the first case, no records existed that would have allowed traceability of the farm or region where wool was originally produced. Documents seen for wool coming from individual farms indicated the region of origin. Commercial documentation accompanying the wool to washers in Belgium or France did not include information on ABP as required in Annex II to the ABP Regulation (16). 9 In the food processing establishments visited (meat, milk, retail and wholesale) it was noted that generally there were established systems for handling of ABP. In the meat industry the system was well established in respect of the handling of category 1 and 2 materials. These ABP were mixed together and sent to a category 1 processing plant, as foreseen. Some deficiencies were noted in connection to their handling: (15) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that the two customers in question were dealers who collected the material and delivered it to its ultimate destination. These dealers also had their own approved food plant, but the material was not delivered to that address. The ABP Regulation does not stipulate that these dealers must be approved. Approval as an intermediary is not necessary, since the material was not delivered to the food plant and since the approval requirements (building and hygiene requirements) are not applicable to a dealer. The VD recognises this problem and is considering ways of addressing it. The error here was that the wrong destination was given on the commercial documentation. The firms do this deliberately for commercial reasons, as they do not want the recipient/customer to know where the material was purchased from. (16) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that this point will be given particular attention because of the risk of spreading of animal diseases. The tracking and tracing of raw wool needs to be guaranteed. 13 - Some containers were still labelled "SRM" instead of category 1 material (17). - The automatic device for colouring of category 1 material was out of order in one slaughterhouse. - Transport documentation for disposal of category 2 material was without final destination in one establishment producing meat products. 9 In the retail and wholesale sectors, the systems for the collection and disposal of ABP were established on the initiative of the private sector and manuals of procedures had been elaborated. 9 In the distribution centres visited different types of foodstuffs or former foodstuffs were received from the retail outlets. In one of them all the products were in principle regarded as still fit for human consumption and a final decision was only taken in the distribution centre even if the products had expired or the packaging was broken. In another distribution centre this type of material was already considered as unfit at arrival. From the distribution centres the former foodstuffs were sent either to biogas/composting plants or to a category 3 intermediate plant. In one of them, category 2 material was also collected and sent for rendering in a category 1 processing plant using collecting facilities in a nearby facility belonging to the same company and not approved under the ABP Regulation. 9 Other deficiencies noted in the food establishments were related to labelling of containers for final disposal, weighing of ABP before disposal and in respect of commercial documents accompanying the consignments. 9 With respect to the milk industry, the establishment visited had established GMP+ procedures for the handling of ABP, but some products should have been categorised as category 2 or 3 materials. Different types of by-products of the production process were considered for quality reasons all as fit for human consumption until the dispatch of the products for feed mills already as feed, so they were not considered ABP at any moment. 9 An exception from this was milk containing residues. The COKZ and de VWA have between them agreed a procedure as to how to deal with milk in which residues are detected above the statutory limit. 9 No provisions were in place in the slaughterhouses visited regarding any pre- treatment process for the retention and collection of animal material that complies with requirements as laid down in Chapter IX of Annex II to the ABP Regulation. 9 Concerning the category 3 material, companies were largely aware of the allowed uses for this material and of the ways of disposal, but in some establishments additional destinations noted were not in accordance with the ABP Regulation. Variation was noted between establishments in respect of description of procedures to be followed. In some establishments procedures had been established and in other there were no procedures adapted to the ABP produced. The implementation of the procedures for categorisation, (17) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that with regard to the labelling of containers, Chapter I of Annex II to the ABP Regulation states that materials must be identifiable, i.e. that the categories of materials must be identified during collection and transportation. Exactly how this identification must be carried out is not stated. Abattoirs must set clear systems to identify these materials that must be accepted by the relevant CA in compliance with the ABP Regulation. 14 identification, collection and dispatch of this material was less strict than for category 1 and 2 ABP resulting in serious shortcomings identified by the mission team (18): - Bones already considered as category 3 material sent for production of edible gelatine in another Member State. - Lobes of lungs already considered as category 3 material sent for freezing in an establishment approved in accordance with Council Directive 64/433/EEC (19). - One meat products plant carried out a trading business in collecting and selling category 3 materials from slaughterhouses. The documentation relating to these consignments did not indicate the destination or category of this material. In addition, there was no indication that the material was not intended for human consumption.

Application of the approval system for ABP establishments and premises The approval system was largely applied as described, however some shortcomings were noted: Observations: 9 In most of the establishments visited, either approved already or within the transitional period, awareness on ABP issues was good, but some gaps were noted a regards knowledge of the requirements on commercial documentation and of the lists of approved or registered suppliers or customers that applied to many of the plants visited (20). 9 In many of the establishments visited, approval visits had been only recently carried out and evaluation of the ensuing reports was still taking place at the upper administrative levels. Some reports were still under preparation by the relevant inspector (21). 9 The plant processing category 1 material was not approved yet under the ABP Regulation since KvW staff only considered it as a formality because the supervision was considered enough to rule out any problem. In addition, some depots used as intermediate plants for category 1 and 2 materials were not yet (18) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that different measures have been taken to resolve all these shortcomings and, in particular: - As regards the first indent, the establishment in question has applied for registration to supply raw materials for the production of gelatine for human consumption. This application is being processed. - In relation with the second indent, monitoring of the establishment has been stepped up. The lungs are now delivered and frozen for human consumption. The identification and documentation is in order. (19) Council Directive 64/433/EEC of 26 June 1964 on health conditions for the production and marketing of fresh meat - OJ L 121, 29.07.1964, p.2012 . (20) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that it is unclear if it is a shortcoming related to the CCA or to the establishments. Despite all the information issued by the LNV and the CCA, the establishments themselves also have a responsibility to keep up to date with the legislation. The report mentions at an earlier point that the supply of information to the industry is good. (21) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that this is questionable as a shortcoming. Many establishments were being visited around that time or had already been visited and were awaiting their definitive approval. The administrative processing of an approval also takes time. 15 approved, and staff from KvW declared that they had not had the time to do it. These were considered low priority as they were already controlled under previous legislation. More priority had been given to approval of the incinerators for pet animals that were not yet under control. No decision had yet been taken on how often these intermediate plants would have to be inspected by staff from the KvW regional offices. 9 Not all technical plants and incineration plants for dead pets, not approved under previous legislation, were yet approved according to new ABP provisions. 9 No plant had yet been officially validated by the CCA according to Chapter V of Annex V to the ABP regulation; nevertheless, all the plants visited by the mission team were largely applying the requirements as laid down in the EU requirements on this area. 9 Some of the plants allegedly approved and asked to be visited by the mission team turned out to have discontinued their operation some time ago without it having been notified to or noted by any CA yet. 9 The RVV inspector in charge of the supervision in the collection centre mentioned in section 2.4.1, and despite the deficiencies noted, had given positive advice in August 2004 for the approval of the establishment under the ABP Regulation. This positive advice was a common finding in other plants also in spite of the deficiencies noted in relation with inappropriate commercial documentation (22).

Application of official controls and supervision along the ABP chain Official controls and supervision were largely applied as described, particularly as regards: 9 A very good supervision was noted at visiting the BIP in one harbour with respect to imports of ABP, channelling of rejected consignments till their destruction in the processing plant for category 1 material and control on proper disposal of international catering waste. Meetings were held weekly between staff involved in these issues with regular attendance of policy officials from the RVV central service to update and clarify legal and administrative procedures. 9 KvW inspectors responsible for the category 1 processing plant carried out a good supervision of the reconciliation of the inflow and outflow of unprocessed and processed ABP. Five times a year, one of the inspectors cross- checked the amounts received in the plant with RVV inspectors responsible for the establishments of origin. No major problem was ever found. 9 Transport of MBM and rendered fats from category 1 material to power plants in The Netherlands was kept under good supervision by the KvW inspectors. As regards part of this material sent for incineration to Germany, RVV (22) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that shortcomings relating to commercial documentation are no obstacle to the obtaining of an approval, since commercial documentation is not an approval requirement. The only exception to this rule is the approval requirements for collection centres. 16 inspectors were responsible for its control and arrival of the consignments was confirmed with an ANIMO message. 9 Controls on the meat sector were well documented in respect of category 1 and 2 materials using the standard routine checklists and the checklists designed for the control of food hygiene provisions in these establishments. However, some shortcomings were also noted: 9 In many of the establishments visited, particularly as regards category 3 material, supervision of the reconciliation of the inflow and outflow of ABP and products derived therefrom was not a common practice. 9 No input was received by the KvW from the environmental authorities on the actual incineration of the processed category 1 material in power plants in The Netherlands. In the power plant visited they were also incinerating category 3 material; however, no supervision of the arrival or incineration of these ABP was done by either KvW or RVV staff. 9 Supervision of the plants' own checks and HACCP procedures in place was regularly done by RVV or KvW inspectors depending on the category of the ABP involved, but in some plants their implementation was very vague and they did not cover all requirements of the ABP Regulation. 9 In one plant provisionally approved acting as an intermediate for cattle hides, commercial documentation was correctly filled in with information on the category of the fresh or salted pieces. However, RVV inspectors had not noted that their quantity was not included (23). 9 In the fat processing plant (see also section 2.4.1), the RVV inspector advised the mission team that there was no specific checklist for this kind of establishments and that he did not report to his hierarchy on the visits carried out. Deficiencies as regards inappropriate commercial documentation had not been detected and no information exchanged with the officials at the slaughterhouses or cutting plants of origin. recommendations.text: Competent authorities The VWA/RVV is responsible for the import controls at the BIPs. The Customs authorities execute certain import controls, supervise non BIP crossing points and check for illegal imports of veterinary products and live animals. The tasks in relation to these matters are described in an annex of the Agreement between the "Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality" (LNV) and the "Ministry of Finance". The Customs authorities are part of the Ministry of Finance, operating under the "General Directorate for Taxes and Customs Administration". The General Inspection Service (AID) is an inspection and investigation department of the LNV. The AID is competent to enforce the regulations of LNV with a view to prosecution. In general, the AID acts complementary to the other supervising services, both as supervisor and as investigation service. The VWA/KvW is responsible inland for illegally imported consignments in fishery products, milk products and by-products establishments.

Legislative and administrative measures Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 has not yet been implemented. Instructions to customs are outdated. Commission Decision 2002/349/EC(e) has not yet been 2 implemented and the positive list is not fully in accordance to the EU provisions (see also point 5.2.1).

Co-operation between different authorities ¾ The above mentioned agreement describes the co-operation with customs. However, there is no access to customs databases for the veterinary services. ¾ The CCA has no overview for the whole country for the number and quantity of illegal imports seized by customs, including CITES products. ¾ When illegal imports for freight consignments are found inland by RVV or customs the BIP of Rotterdam is informed and the consignments are seized and rejected. ¾ Co-operation with airport authorities is not efficient e.g. apart from outdated posters no other information means are used (e.g. leaflets, in-flight announcements) as airport authorities are reluctant to co-operate in this. Customs carried out checks for consignments sent by post and some consignments (about 0.5%) were scanned. There was no information about the controls carried out for personal baggage at ports points of entry (no posters had been distributed) and customs make surveillance checks to the port areas but not for the boats arriving(2). ¾ Co-ordination with municipalities, which are responsible for displaying posters at the points of entry, was not adequate. The CCA had not yet informed the municipalities about the posters to be displayed at all points of entry(3). 5.2. CHECKS ON ILLEGAL IMPORTS "Illegal imports" in the context of this report, is the introduction onto the territory of the Community of products of animal origin or live animals which, either accidentally or intentionally, have not been subject to, and cleared following, the veterinary checks foreseen in Community legislation. 5.2.1. Organisation and operation of Customs ¾ Customs control the personal luggage and post sent to private persons based on an instruction from the "Ministry of Finance". There are 37 entry points from third countries (17 airports and 20 ports). Customs give the passenger the option for voluntary abandonment of the goods for personal consumption and the passengers sign a voluntary abandon declaration that is registered by customs. If the passenger does not abandon the goods voluntarily, customs pass the case to the veterinary authorities of the VWA/RVV for further prosecution. ¾ There is a customs database for seized personal baggage consignments. However, there was no detailed information for the controls carried out at each of the relevant points of entry in the Netherlands according to Regulation (EC) (2) In their response to the draft report the Netherlands CCA noted that customs carry out checks on boats arriving by employment of the "integral control strategy"; depending on the goods involved these checks also include veterinary aspects. (3) In their response to the draft report the Netherlands CCA noted that the municipalities are not responsible for displaying posters and the VWA/RVV has drawn up a list of the owners and operators of these places of entry. In some cases a municipal port authority is involved, in other cases the airline. 3 No 745/2004, no central Customs authority was responsible for collection of this information, and neither was the information known to the VWA/RVV. ¾ For freight consignments, customs receive before unloading a declaration from the person responsible for the load (D11). Manifests are not received in every customs post (e.g. in Maaslavkte) and when received (e.g. in Reeweg) these are pre-selected by the person responsible for the load. No pre-notification in the form of CVED is received before arrival, only the D 11 is received by customs. BIP staff has no access to the customs database, and no cross checks of the manifests are carried out with pre-notifications. ¾ The customs system "SAGITTA" is not completely updated to flag all TARIC codes (e.g. 9705 game trophies, 0511 unprocessed manure), which require veterinary checks as the positive list of the Decision 2002/349/EC has not yet been implemented. Consignments are only cross checked against the SAGITTA when an import procedure is opened. CN codes of the positive list are not used for the selection by Customs who select the consignments for veterinary checks based on the shipping agent description of the consignment(4). For consignments in transit/transhipment there is no customs database and no cross- check of the TARIC codes with the requirement for veterinary checks. For transhipments for import to other Member States the D 51 document is only on paper. ¾ CITES products and live animals are under customs control. Customs stated that in case of doubts for products they inform the AID of the LNV who are responsible. For live animals Customs inform RVV to send the live animals in quarantine. ¾ Customs stated that once per week 1 illegal CITES consignment is found in Amsterdam airport and seized and rejected by Customs. 5.2.2. Imports of products for personal consumption 5.2.2.1.Background Customs are responsible for personal baggage checks of travellers. Customs stated that they control all points of entry (all flights from third countries and the only existing post centre in Amsterdam Schiphol). ¾ There was no information given about the training carried out for customs in the field of veterinary checks and checks for illegal imports of veterinary consignments. 5.2.2.2.Information to passengers/travellers ¾ Posters are displayed in the airports visited but the CCA has difficulties in particular at the airports, to enable provision of other means of information to the passengers in order to increase public awareness. Air transport operators have not agreed to make in-flight announcements, neither are leaflets distributed to passengers. The CCA stated that leaflets are only available in the Dutch representations (Agricultural Councils) and in travel agencies in the third countries. It is not ensured that the posters are displayed in all points of entry from third countries (e.g. not in ports). (4) In their response to the draft report the Netherlands CCA noted that it is in fact not possible to make use of CN codes for the selection of the consignments, as these CN codes are not supplied by the agents. 4 ¾ The posters used are not updated and do not contain all the information foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. 5.2.2.3.Organisation of controls/sanctions ¾ Customs are not permanently present in every point of entry from third countries either BIP or non-BIP. However, customs stated that in case of the airports all arriving flights from third countries in all points of entry are checked by customs and international flights from other EU airports are checked on a risk basis in the same way as in Amsterdam airport and the same checks are carried out for the consignments sent by post. ¾ There was no information available about the checks carried out for personal luggage at the ports, either BIPs or non-BIP points of entry. There are no checks organised in the ports where only a general surveillance of the port area is carried out by a specific team but not for the boats arriving (e.g. in Rotterdam port customs in the framework of integrated control have 3 patrol cars operating during day and 2 during the night). Checks in ships were carried out only in case of suspicion. ¾ The CCA and Customs did not know how many consignments were seized in the individual points of entry for the whole country. Customs have a database for abandoned consignments which can be accessed only locally. The CCA did not have access and no central authority has been assigned to gather the results of the checks. ¾ There were no records for cases of consignments not abandoned by passengers in the whole country. The same applies for CITES for which the CCA had an overview for the seized consignments of live animals but not for products. ¾ Passengers are neither liable for the cost of destruction of seized consignments nor for any penalties as required by Article 4 paragraph 3 of Regulation 745/2004 and in Article 17(5) of Directive 97/78/EC, if the illegal consignments are abandoned after being discovered by customs. At a BIP-airport-entry-point (Amsterdam airport) Customs use scanning equipment to check selected baggage. Sniffer dogs are not employed to check for products of animal origin. As part of their integrated controls customs physically check about 5% of all baggage from all flights from third countries (3.5% opened and 1.5% scanned). In case of reinforced control for a risk flight customs raise this percentage to 10% (7% opened and 3% scanned). In case of high risk flights customs carry out 100% check of personal baggage for specific countries. The same percentages of checks are carried out by customs for packages, which are sent by post. Interline baggage of passengers from third countries with stopover in other EU airports are checked at the destination airport in the Netherlands. In this case no manifests of the arriving passengers are received and their baggage check is based on the coloured tags of the baggage, which is different for passengers who started their trip from third countries. Customs have their own criteria and use a risk based approach for all kind of illegal consignments (e.g. tobacco, drugs, weapons, veterinary products). ¾ In this framework there is no priority given for veterinary products as these are included in the general illegal imports checks. Customs stated that for veterinary products personal luggage checks are taking into consideration an instruction from the "Ministry of Finance" with non accepted products and countries after information received from VWA/RVV. However, this 5 instruction has not yet been updated as the last instruction which was found at local customs was from 27 January 2003 and the list of products and countries as well as the posters used was not in accordance to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. ¾ Seized consignments are incinerated; however, Customs do not receive confirmation for the delivery of the seized consignments to a company nor do they receive feedback from the place of destruction(5). It was not known if such records are kept. It was not clarified if the incinerator used for the destruction of the consignments is approved in accordance to Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002. In 2003 for this airport 4924 illegal consignments (34.5 tons) were found by customs in personal luggage checks. In addition one consignment was not abandoned and RVV prosecuted the case at the Court. There was an overview of CITES consignments of live animals, dead animals and products seized by customs during 2003. At a non-BIP-airport-entry-point there were passengers with baggage from third countries arriving directly from third countries or through other EU airports (interline). Customs do not receive manifests of passengers from third countries in particular those with stop-over in other EU-airports and only the colour label is used to identify the interline baggage from third countries. Interline baggage are checked at a percentage of 80%. For flights from third countries about 5% of baggage is opened per flight and 5-10% of baggage is scanned. About 40 kg of illegal imports are found per week. However, no detailed information of the seized consignments in 2003 was provided. ¾ Customs stated that all arriving flights are checked by them who are present when the flights arrive. For Customs the priorities for passenger personal baggage checks for veterinary products are the same as in the BIP-airport-entry point. The last instructions for illegal imports were sent from the "Ministry of Finance" on 30.01.2003 and the list of products and countries was not in accordance to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. ¾ The poster in this airport was sent from another airport (Amsterdam airport). It is not updated, only in Dutch and Turkish language, not in accordance to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. No in-flight announcements are made by air transport operators and there is no legal base for the authorities to enforce it. In the past air transport operators were reluctant to distribute brochures for Avian influenza to passengers from Asian countries although an in-flight video was played. ¾ The seized consignments were put in an unsecured waste bin outside the airport area. There were no documents for the delivery and feedback from the destruction of seized consignments(6). (5) In their response to the draft report the Netherlands CCA noted that the task of customs is confined to identifying illegal consignments and subsequent action such as destruction and administrative follow up is the responsibility of the VWA/RVV. 6 5.2.3. Import and transit of freight ¾ The system is developed for imported freight consignments, but not for transit/transhipment as described under point 5.2.1 4th indent. The selection of the consignments subject to veterinary checks is not completely reliable and consignments may escape veterinary checks as it is not based on an updated positive list as required by the EU provisions and relies largely on declaration by the forwarding agent without cross checks of pre-notifications with the manifests by the official veterinarian. ¾ Physical checks of the consignments to verify the information declared on the D11 are carried out by Customs, using a risk based system. At the time of unloading on a D11 form about 0.5% of the consignments are scanned. If the scan raises doubts, the consignment is also physically checked. Additionally, another 3% of import consignments are physically checked on a risk analysis basis. There were no details of checks and seized consignments found inland by customs or RVV for the whole country for 2003 for freight consignments. However, in 1 BIP the BIP staff stated that they are informed by Customs or RVV inland that about 1 freight consignment per month are found to pass the border without veterinary checks.

ADDENDUM The Dutch Authorities commented on the draft report by a letter dated 18 April 2006. They noted their disagreement with the FVO's assessment that KDS is a control body as defined in Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, article 5. The Dutch Authorities stated that KDS has no control over the way in which its employees and contracted workers carry out their work as official auxiliaries. This control is exclusively in the hands of the VWA. This also means that the VWA does not delegate inspection tasks to KDS. As in the view of the Dutch Authorities KDS cannot be considered to be a control body, the Commission was not notified of KDS and the tasks delegated to it. recommendations.text: To provide information to the Commission services on the new structure of the competent authority in order to ensure that information in TRACES for intra-Union trade correctly corresponds to the local veterinary units listed in

citations.text: The NVWA is the competent authority responsible for coordination of the use of TRACES in accordance with the requirements of Article 1 of Decision 92/486/EEC. In 2012, the structure of the NVWA was changed, which has led to the removal of the local veterinary units (LVUs) and the regions. The information on the structural changes has not been provided to the Commission in order to amend Decision 2009/821/EC. This has an impact on the use of TRACES. Currently, the official veterinarians issuing INTRA-CERTs access TRACES as the central competent authority (not as local veterinary units listed in Decision 2009/821/EC) in order to reflect the existing structure of the NVWA. The audit team noted that all INTRA-CERTs in TRACES identify the non-existing local veterinary units. This is due to economic operators accessing the system using the postal code of the region in the Netherlands following the old structure of the local veterinary units. The NVWA expressed awareness of its obligation to provide updated information to the Commission on the amendment of Decision 2009/821/EC.

The set-up of the competent authority in TRACES does not correspond to the current structure where local veterinary units of the NVWA following regional division have been removed. Therefore, all INTRA-CERTs in TRACES identify the non-existent local veterinary units. The competent authority has suitably qualified and experienced staff for TRACES activities.

responses.response: Proposal for the new structure of the competent authority was submitted to DG SANTE / TRACES-Team on 3 April 2015 and was voted in SCOPAFF of 16/17 April 2015. Implementation will be realized in cooperation with the TRACES team.

recommendations.text: To ensure that data of relevant official controls (e.g. exit transit, re-imported or destruction consignments, controls at abattoirs, intra-EU movements of certain animal by-products) are recorded in TRACES as laid down in Decision

citations.text: Repeated non-confirmation of exit of transit consignments was noted, even though the work instructions issued by the NVWA require the confirmation of the exit of transit consignments within 30 working days as required by Article 9 of Directive 91/496/EC and Articles 11 and 12(8) of Directive 97/78/EC. In the Rotterdam BIP visited, the transit consignments were followed-up using shipping companies' IT systems to check if they left the port and that information was recorded in TRACES. The Amsterdam BIP visited does not have a follow-up system to track exit transit consignments and does not record them in TRACES.

Commercial operators pre-notify consignments exiting the warehouse using hard copy CVEDs. After veterinary checks, consignments are accompanied using hard copy CVEDs completed and signed manually by official veterinarians. These CVEDs are entered manually into TRACES by correctly using the split function, when the veterinary officials are not overloaded with veterinary checks at the warehouses. This means that some consignments are notified to the BIPs in other Member States via TRACES with a delay. As a result, those consignments can leave the EU territory without the exit BIP being able to perform the controls. The risk is mitigated since the veterinary authorities communicate with other Member States and Dutch Customs in all cases when confirmation is not received.

National instructions issued by the NVWA require the confirmation of arrival for re- imported consignments in accordance with the requirements of Article 15 of Directive 97/78/EC. However, TRACES-NL does not identify those consignments for follow-up by the veterinary inspectors at the place of destination and it is not recorded in TRACES. Re-imported consignments might be higher risk, especially if they were rejected by the third countries because of bacterial or chemical contamination. The reasons of rejection by third countries of products of animal origin produced in the Netherlands might need to be investigated.

Consignments sent for destruction are not followed up by the veterinary inspectors at the place of destination due to the set-up of the risk module in TRACES-NL. TRACES-NL does not classify those consignments as high risk and does not require them to be followed up at the place of destination contrary to the requirements of Article 17(2b) of Directive 97/78/EC. 5.2.8 Signatures

In relation to the movement of live animals from other Member States: INTRA-CERTs and CVEDs are downloaded into TRACES-NL and are filtered for official controls if this foreseen by the national risk evaluation plan. Approximately 8 percent of consignments of live animals are physically controlled at the destination (except for some live animals from several Member States where controls are carried out on 100 percent of consignments) following the requirements of Article 5(a) of Directive 90/425/EC on non-discriminatory checks. Those controls are correctly recorded in TRACES. Official controls related to ante-mortem inspections are recorded in TRACES following the frequency of 8 percent identified by TRACES-NL. The competent authority stated that the reduction in controls is due to limited human and financial resources. Even though the controls are carried out at the abattoirs, they are not recorded in TRACES contrary to the requirements of Article 2(a) of Decision 2004/292/EC. The audit team followed several cases where staff of the Agriculture and Nature Division of the NVWA carried out animal welfare controls en route and at the place of destination. Those controls were routinely recorded in TRACES as required by Article 2(a) of Decision 2004/292/EC. 5.2.10 DOCOM module

The instructions mentioned in finding 41 describe requirements on the controls to be carried out at the place of destination when certain animal by-products arrive from other Member States. Those instructions require that the controls of certain animal by- products shall be carried out on an average of 10 percent of consignments contrary to the requirement of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The competent authority stated that the reduction in controls is due to limited human and financial resources, and the high number of animal by-products arriving from other Member States.

The use of TRACES for routine activities for imports and for intra-Union movements of live animals leaving the Netherlands is in general correct. Lack of records in TRACES reflects lack of controls by the BIPs (e.g. exit of transit consignments) or by the NVWA offices (e.g. re-imported or consignments sent for destruction). In some cases these controls are done, but not recorded in TRACES. The arrival of a number of intra-Union consignments is not controlled at the place of destination (e.g. animal by- products) or the full range of controls are not recorded in TRACES (e.g. slaughter animals). Therefore, the traceability of consignments mentioned above and the communication between the competent authorities of Member States is undermined. 11

recommendations.text: To further develop the system of official controls on traceability, labelling and the use of additives so as to meet the requirements set out in Articles 3.1 (risk based frequency of controls) and 8.1 (documented procedures and instructions) and 10 (control methods) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and to monitor and verify compliance with Article 18.1 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002.

citations.text: Specific checklists for controls on traceability and labelling are in use. However no checklists or sampling reports of meat products were available on the use of additives. The V&I checklist for traceability and labelling (effective from 15-02-2015) does not 4 contain detailed questions on internal traceability and quantitative traceability (mass balance). In-depth verification of traceability within establishments is rarely performed.
The CA did not have a special checklist or instructions for checking the use of additives. Evidence of official sampling was not available in the establishments visited.

The Dutch CA has clarified their position in a note to the DG Health & Food Safety dated 3 June 2015 concerning internal traceability, pointing out that neither Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 nor the Commission Guidance on the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 European law imposes any obligations on FBOs to have an internal traceability system, and that, as a consequence, the NVWA cannot impose requirements in this regard. The only exception concerns the traceability of beef.

The requirement that FBOs must be able to demonstrate from whom products are received and to whom products are delivered is checked and enforced. However, if the mass balance (correlation of quantities received with output of final product, quantities in-storage and production losses) is not correct, or absent, no follow-up actions are taken and no sanctions can be imposed.

A control system is in place and developments to improve mechanisms for detection of fraud and traceability control are in progress. Within the scope of the audit, the official control plans are implemented as foreseen and official controls are carried out in accordance with documented procedures. However, controls on traceability are not sufficiently thorough and controls on the use of additives are inadequate. Staff have not received effective training on the issues covered by this audit. 5.2.2. Implementation of official controls

The audit team verified the documentation of these 12 files. The outcome of this exercise was as follows: Qualitative tracing (one step backwards, one step forwards) was satisfactory in all cases. In 4 out of 12 cases, the correlation of quantities along the production chain was satisfactory. In the other eight, the CA did not verify the amount produced against the raw material intake, the product recipes, the technical specifications of the additives and spice mixtures used. The absence of reliable production sheets was noted. Many commercial documents were not fully compliant with the requirements set out in in Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 931/2011. The CA did not verify that dispatch documents contained sufficient information (lot number, batch no., description) to reliably link the consignment with the documentation. 7 In one sample the tracing of the additives had not been possible due to the large number of additives.

The audit team selected five out of the twelve files for on-the-spot verification of the data provided by the CA. The outcome of this exercise was as follows: Qualitative tracing was satisfactory in three out of five cases. However correlation of quantities (received, used, in-stock, dispatched) was not conclusive in any of the five cases. When checked in detail, inconsistencies, which had not been identified by the CA, were found. In the five cases, the team confirmed the evaluation by the CA that the food labelling was not compliant. In addition the audit team identified that: A sample of meat was named "kogelbiefstuk" (topside), giving the impression that it was "fresh meat" however the label on the back indicated that it was a meat preparation due to the addition of additives to prolong shelf life and to correct the decolouration. Such a description is misleading to consumers. In addition the label on the product indicated the presence of stabiliser E415 however this additive only had a function in the marinade used. In one meat product (sample file verified on-the-spot), E412 was used without technical justification and was not mentioned on the label. The FBO stated that this additive will no longer be used for this product. During the tracing of one product, the CA had not identified that the same production code was used for products already produced and to be used in the future with the same intermediate product. In the freezer store, 200 kg of intermediate product was stored and was not included in the mass balance calculation. Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain

Impressive resources had been mobilised to facilitate this audit and to trace the 12 samples. However, the outcome of the traceability exercises conducted by the audit team within this audit demonstrates that controls are not sufficiently rigorous to detect some important deficiencies, in particular, in relation to accounting for all meat and ingredients used and to information on commercial documents and labelling. 5.2.2.2.Official controls on Food Business Operators' obligations Audit findings

Within planned CA visits, the time normally allocated for the CA comprehensive controls on the labelling and traceability is much shorter than the time used for the tracing of the 12 samples during this exercise. This could explain that, contrary to the findings during this audit, the results of most planned inspections did not indicate systemic non compliances regarding traceability, labelling and use of additives.

The audit team noted shortcomings in relation to follow-up of deficiencies in some of the establishments visited. In one establishment, in particular, the CA had noted significant shortcomings in relation to traceability and critical control points but these had not been addressed during follow-up visits.

In one establishment the audit team identified the presence of eight bags of dried blood without identification. The provider of dried blood had a procedure to remove all labels (including identification marks, process codes, use-by-date, etc.) from product supplied. The CA informed the DG Health & Food Safety that, while a warning had been issued to the provider of the dried blood, no further action had been taken. (see also paragraph 39 fourth sub indent).

Control of incoming goods: In three establishments visited, some meat and meat products had been accepted without the required health mark or identification mark. In one of them (a large distribution centre), in the reception area three consignments out of six were not compliant. In a cutting plant, the individual commercial documents of the incoming consignments from one supplier did not correspond with the content of the corresponding truck. A difference of 200 half pig carcasses was noted on three consignments. The FBO control at entry did not identify these discrepancies. A similar discrepancy (altering of commercial documentation to correct a significant weight difference) had been noted by the audit team in the file of one of the samples selected for the traceability exercise (see paragraph 27) where the same cutting plant was involved. In a cold store the procedure for control at reception for chilled and frozen products was not sufficiently thorough. A wrong batch number was attributed and, although it had been identified that a consignment had an elapsed use-by-date and was blocked in the system, other inaccuracies in the documentation were not noticed during entry control. 9 The FBO had accepted the dried blood (see paragraph 37) without any comments and stated that the procedure for the control of the incoming ingredients did not include the verification of the labelling. The CA informed the audit team that an inspection would be initiated the following week.

Traceability systems: In one establishment visited the FBO had no traceability procedures in place: products were registered but without any link to the individual consignment such as production dates or codes, batch numbers, the accompanying documents. Although during a previous inspection, the CA had identified that traceability was inadequate, no follow-up on this non-compliance had been carried out. During the visit the CA stated that a fine would be issued for this non-compliance. In several establishments, some products were unidentified and there were open packages without identification. In a number of cases, quantities of raw materials, product in stock, and product dispatched did not correlate. In other cases, the information available did not allow a reliable calculation: e.g. absence of internal traceability records; quantities based on estimates which did not take into account produce not meeting specification (sent for re-work); anomalies in calculation of use-by dates. In one cutting plant, an employee did not follow the FBO's own traceability procedures: the procedure for traceability of pig meat was used instead of that for bovine meat. The consequence was that a batch of beef meat exceeded more than one day's production, contrary to the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1825/2000. In addition, the FBO's procedure for pig meat had not yet been adapted in line with the requirements of Regulation (EU) No 1337/2013. One operator used the same production code for products already produced and to be used in the future with the same intermediate product. This could lead to products with the same product codes and different use by dates. In one case, the FBO own procedures for determining shelf-life and use-by-dates was imprecise and, in any case, was not followed. In several establishments, old obsolete labels were still present on plastic crates, causing confusion on the origin of the products.

Use of additives: In one establishment, according to the recipe of one non-heat treated meat product, the content of nitrite to be used was above the legal limit set out in Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008. Specifications, on several additive pre-mixes seen, did not mention the content of the additives for which a maximum limit is established and consequently this does not allow calculation of the maximal amount to be used. Official controls do not include checks on the use of additives.

The significant non-compliances in one establishment raises question as to the efficacy of the official controls in this particular case. Concerning the many non-compliances relating to the incoming goods, while none of them can be considered as critical, their range and frequency indicate that, notwithstanding the official system in place, controls are superficial and unable to detect any systemic non- compliances regarding traceability (particularly with regard to quantities) and labelling. A contributing factor is the insufficient time allocated for checks on traceability during official controls. No systematic official controls are performed on the use of food additives by FBOs.
The absence of official controls on the flow of product through establishments undermines the effectiveness of the overall system of traceability.

The Dutch CA considers that for the production of MSM ("type 4") with reference to point 4 Chapter III, Section IV of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, there is no time limit between deboning and production of MSM. The FBO producer of MSM visited restricts the use of the poultry carcasses to five days after slaughter because they produce only "type 4", but has no indication if the three days between slaughter and cutting had been respected in all cases. In addition, the use by date (three days) of the 11 deboned poultry carcasses fixed by a German supplier was ignored by this FBO and had expired. The CA undertook to follow-up this issue.

audits.title: evaluate the official controls on consignments in transit

recommendations.text: To ensure that instructions on the replacement of certificates are documented as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The audit team noted that Customs officials perform the documentary checks using a database which contains up to date and relevant information on requirements for transit consignments. The models of transit/storage veterinary certificates uploaded in the above-mentioned database are correct and comply with the model established by EU legislation. However, the audit team noted that a number of these certificates additionally bear the footnotes referring to the draft document number provided during the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed. This leads to discrepancies between the certificates accompanying the consignments and the model in the database. There is no documented procedure explaining either to Customs officers or to BIP staff how to handle the veterinary certificates issued by third countries which do not bear the above-mentioned footnotes, contrary to the requirements of Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The BIP staff explained that Customs officers would contact the BIP staff if the information in the veterinary certificate was unclear or if deficiencies were detected.

BIP staff stated that, when officials detect errors in the certificates, explanatory letters from the third country competent authority were routinely requested. The NVWA 4 confirmed that replacement certificates are rarely requested. Despite the absence of EU legislation on this matter, the Guidelines for Design, Production, Issuance and Use of Generic Official Certificates (CAC/GL 38-2001), issued by the Codex Alimentarius Commission, indicate that, for certain administrative corrections or if the certificates are lost or damaged, replacement certificates are foreseen. This is also reflected in the Guidance on transit. The BIP operational procedures do not indicate when explanatory letters can be accepted and when replacement certificates should be requested instead.

The veterinary checks for transit consignments at the entry BIP are implemented ensuring that consignments in transit fulfil the necessary animal health guarantees. The fact that the NVWA accepts explanatory letters when discrepancies are found during documentary checks weakens the effectiveness of the documentary controls. 5.2.2 Controls at warehouses and ship suppliers 5.2.2.1 Approval and listing of the warehouses/ship suppliers and specially approved warehouses

recommendations.text: To ensure the official controls are appropriate and effective in verifying the traceability of the consignments stored in the customs/free warehouses/ship suppliers as required by the Article 4(2)(a) Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The warehouse operators identify each box of the consignment stored in the warehouse with a label with the reference number of the arriving CVED, in accordance with the requirement of Article 1(5) of Decision 2000/571/EC. In addition, the information on the consignments stored in the warehouse is recorded in the operators' databases, in accordance with the requirements of Article 3(1) of the same Decision. Nevertheless, the audit team noted discrepancies in the traceability of consignments stored (see finding 36).

The audit team conducted traceability exercises both to trace back and trace forward a randomly selected consignment stored in the warehouse. The audit team noted the following: In one warehouse, the warehouse operator incorrectly recorded the country of origin of the product stored in the warehouse (i.e. the country of origin of the product was Canada, but it was recorded in the operator's database as Argentina). In the other warehouse, the records were correct but the boxes stored displayed labels with an incorrect CVED number.

The official staff responsible for the official controls at the warehouses perform weekly verification of the consignments stored in the warehouse concerned. The audit team noted that during these verification visits the information on the selected consignments 8 is obtained from the warehouse operators' databases and it is cross-checked with the number of boxes stored in the warehouse. Official staff do not compare the data of the operator with official data available (e.g. amounts entering and exiting the warehouse). Therefore, the verification activities are not appropriate to identify the deficiencies described in finding 36, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.2.3 Movement from the free/customs warehouses to the exit border inspection post

There is a well-functioning system of official controls on consignments in transit upon entry or exit from warehouses and ship suppliers which ensures that if a consignment has been manipulated during transit or does not arrive at the warehouse, this will be detected. Consignments ready for dispatch are subject to official controls. The controls during the storage are limited and do not include reconciliation exercises, which may potentially compromise the overall system of official controls at the warehouses. 5.2.3 Controls at the exit border inspection post

audits.title: evaluate the application of re-enforced checks on imported products of animal origin

recommendations.text: To ensure that the planning process for the preparation of the monitoring plan for imported goods is risk based as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The Veterinary and Import Division and the Consumer and Safety Division of NVWA are responsible for the planning of the monitoring plan on imported food of animal origin. The NVWA described that both divisions meet after the drafting of the monitoring plan and agree on the implementation at the BIPs. The NVWA stated that for the preparation of the following year's monitoring plan it takes into account RASFF information, quantities of imports, requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, general information on problematic products and advice of the Office for Risk Assessment within the NVWA. There is no evidence that non-compliances not recorded in RASFF (e.g. consignments rejected at the borders due to discrepancies found during documentary checks) are considered in the risk assessment. The meetings or other discussions covering the technical side of the monitoring plan (e.g. risk identification and assessment) are not documented (see finding 6).

The monitoring plan includes residues of veterinary medicines, contaminants and microbiological examination (mainly Salmonella). The NVWA could not demonstrate that its controls are risk-based and did not present any risk assessment or other rationale for the design of the plan (e.g. for testing Trichinella in horse meat, beta-agonists in chicken meat or for excluding from testing honey or egg products, for which the Netherlands is the main country of introduction into the EU). In the absence of any such assessment, the NVWA is not in position to ensure that official controls are carried out on a risk basis as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see finding 1).

Whilst there is a monitoring plan in place, the absence of a risk-based rationale for the design and content of the plan does not ensure that the plan covers all relevant commodities and the related risks. 5.1.2 Implementation of the monitoring plan

recommendations.text: To carry out veterinary checks in order to confirm or rule out suspicion that the EU legislation has not been complied with, following the procedure of Article 24 and in accordance with Article 20 of Council Directive 97/78/EC.

citations.text: Samples under "special projects" (see finding 5) are taken during physical checks at the BIPs, but they are not recorded in TRACES. The NVWA informed the audit team that these samples give an overview for specific commodities, and there are no enforcement actions in case of non-compliances (e.g. rejections, recalls, RASFF notifications). The reason presented was the big delay between the sampling and testing and the limited possibility of the product still being present on the market. BIP staff are not made aware of the results of these tests or of the outcome of the project. This lack of information undermines the ability of the BIP staff to use the intelligence gathered to better inform their actions when assessing the risks associated with imported consignments. There is no evidence that the NVWA uses the results of these "special projects" to improve the following year's monitoring plan.

The procedures in place allow for the possibility of BIP staff to take actions in case of suspicion (including detention and sampling) in accordance with Article 20 of Directive 97/78/EC. However, in practice this is limited to the consignments which are subject to various EU safeguard decisions. These controls are correctly recorded as "Suspicion" in box 28 of the CVEDPs and consignments are detained until the laboratory test results are received.

There is a system in place which could allow BIP staff to take samples in case of suspicion. However, in practice, cases of suspicion where samples are taken are limited only to consignments which are already subject to EU safeguard decisions. The absence of sample collection in regard to any consignment other than the ones subject to EU safeguard decision, together with the limited scope of the monitoring plan, undermines the effectiveness of the official control system.

The instruction on re-enforced checks issued by the Veterinary and Import Division of the NVWA requires that BIP staff take samples following the requirements of re- enforced checks for the next ten consignments as required by Article 24 of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 30 of Council Directive 96/23/EC. The instruction explicitly excludes any further sampling of subsequent consignments (i.e. from the 11th to 30th consignment). This policy decision is contrary to the objective of Article 20 of Directive 97/78/EC which requires the competent authority to carry out any veterinary checks that it deems appropriate in order to confirm or rule out suspicion. 8

The competent authority's decision not to apply re-enforced checks on consignments falling between the 11th to 30th is not in line with the Guidance on re-enforced checks and does not fulfil the objective of the legislation to confirm or rule out suspicion. This approach also has an impact on the consistency of the controls at EU level, as consignments that would normally undergo detention, and possibly testing, in the rest of the Member States do not undergo these controls in the Dutch BIPs.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the coordination between competent authorities and the information available to laboratories and reporting officers allow that the available Salmonella isolates, from the populations specified in point 1 (a) of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, are gathered and subject to antimicrobial susceptibility testing, in order to achieve the minimum number required by point 2.2 and comply with Article 2(2)(a) of the said Decisio 15

citations.text: Nevertheless, the methods used to allocate responsibilities to the different competent authorities and laboratories involved, and the information available to the laboratories and reporting officers, did not allow the gathering and identification of the relevant Salmonella isolates for the populations required by point 1(a) of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. As a consequence, the available Salmonella isolates were not tested and/or reported (see points 22 and 25) in order to achieve the minimum number required. 1 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL 3 Conclusions on the competent authority

The competent authorities responsible for the monitoring of AMR are clearly designated, adequately organised and have the necessary powers for the implementation of the harmonised monitoring of AMR. Nevertheless, there are gaps in the allocation of tasks and in the information available to the different authorities involved in the gathering, selection and testing of Salmonella isolates. These gaps had a negative impact on achieving the Decision 2013/652/EU targets for these bacteria.

In 2014, the competent authority did not report any Salmonella isolates obtained at farm level for the three categories requested by Decision 2013/652/EU (broilers, laying hens and turkeys), despite their availability. The competent authority stated that some of the reported isolates may have originated from samples taken in the context of the SNCP but the flow of information does not allow distinguishing them from isolates from other origins.

Data on the isolates provided by the RIVM do not include information regarding the sampling programme/context, which does not allow the NRL for AMR to ensure that an adequate selection of isolates is subject to AST. As a consequence, all the reported Salmonella isolates were identified as obtained from caeca at slaughterhouses while their origin was unknown.

The RIVM is responsible for the selection of isolates that are submitted to the NRL for AMR for AST. However, the RIVM only gathers a small amount of isolates obtained under the SNCP. This is not in accordance with the technical requirements of point 2.3.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU as, if available, Salmonella isolates obtained in the framework of the national control programmes shall be collected to achieve the minimum number required.

The Agriculture and Nature division of the NVWA oversights the SNCP. The official samples taken within the SNCP are tested in the Animal Health laboratory. The isolates obtained have not been subject to AST so far, since the NVWA staff with responsibilities over the SNCP were not aware, before this audit, of the provisions of Decision 2013/652/EU that requires subjecting these isolates to AST. 2 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=3245 6

The Salmonella isolates obtained from the official samples taken in the context of testing and verification of compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 were gathered and subject to AST but the results were not reported to EFSA, as required by points 1 (a) and 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. The NVWA stated that the AST results for these Salmonella isolates were excluded from reporting to EFSA because the isolate information available in the database to the reporting officers was insufficient to allow, for example, the exclusion of repeated epidemiological units.

In the three slaughterhouses visited the audit team noted that the food business operator's private laboratories regularly obtained Salmonella isolates. Contrary to point 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, these isolates were not gathered by the competent authority despite the fact that the official isolates available were not sufficient to achieve the minimum required (see point 11). recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling at slaughterhouses is representative, as set out by Article 2(1) and points 2.3 and 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, namely by allocating samples on the basis of domestically produced animals, randomly selecting sampling dates and avoid repeatedly sampling the same epidemiological units.

citations.text: Nevertheless, and contrary to point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU, the allocation was not made on the basis of the annual throughput of domestically produced meat. For example, in the poultry slaughterhouse visited the audit team was informed that over 60% of the broilers slaughtered originated from other Member States.

However, the audit team noted the following: NVWA laboratory: o Despite the fact that the laboratory performed investigations of unusual results of MIC determination, the documented procedures in place did not detail these situations specifying the actions to be taken. o There were no procedures in place, in line with ISO 20776-1:2006 and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) M07-A10, to perform colony counts on inoculum suspensions in order to ensure that the required final inoculum concentration is routinely obtained and therefore the test wells contain an adequate number of cells. o In the cases of sulphonamides and trimethopin the MIC determination was not fully harmonised, following the ISO 20776:2006 standard, between different staff performing the determination. o Incubation time and temperatures for MIC determination were not performed fully according to ISO 20776:2006 and CLSI standards as required by point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. In particular, the time/temperature defined for incubation of Campylobacter, Salmonella and E. coli included deviations, from the above standards, by up to 1ºC and 4 hours. NRL for AMR o Contrary to point 4.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the ESBL testing procedures were not fully in line with the EURL protocol for ESBL-, or AmpC- or carbapenemases-producing E. coli. The incubation time set in the procedures for Salmonella and E. coli MIC determination included deviations from ISO 20776:2006 up to 4 hours. These deviations might have an effect on the MIC values obtained.

Nevertheless, improving the laboratory procedures to ensure full alignment with the incubation times and temperatures set in the relevant standards, would further strengthen the quality of the results obtained.

recommendations.text: To update the current system for certification of approved vehicles so that the vehicles appropriate for weaned and unweaned animals are properly identifiable from the vehicle approval certificates issued in accordance with the template in Chapter IV, Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. nd bullet.

citations.text: Drivers' certificates of competence are issued by the Dutch Driving Test Organisation (Centraal Bureau Rijvaardigheidsbewijzen ­ CBR).

Regarding the vehicle's conditions: the full range of checks carried out by the RDW for a new vehicle approval is also performed when renewing the 5-year approval (Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005); the Dutch certificates of approval currently do not distinguish which vehicles are appropriate for weaned and which are appropriate for unweaned animals, contrarily to what is required by Chapter IV Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This implies that unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animals with the biggest risk being the inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Point 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005). The NVWA indicated that it intends to split the vehicle approval on this basis: one approval for "calves younger than 2 months" and another for "calves over 2 months" (similarly, one for "lambs and kids younger than 6 weeks" and another for "lambs and kids over 6 weeks). This was supposed to start after 1 January 2017, but has been delayed; the new start date is 1 July 2017; the stocking density (Point 2.1 Chapter III, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005) is checked during loading; the presence of an official at 100% of loadings also allows the NVWA to check: o maintenance conditions of the vehicle and space above the animals (Points 1.1. and 1.2 of Chapter II, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005); o appropriate bedding for the animals and suitability of the vehicle's drinking devices for the species and categories of animals that are to be transported (Points 1.2 and 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005).

The current system for certification of approved vehicles does not sufficiently distinguish the types of vehicle appropriate for weaned and unweaned animals. As a result unweaned animals may not have access to liquid and be if necessary fed during long distance journeys. The risk of unweaned animals being transported in these unsuitable vehicles is sufficiently mitigated in the Netherlands by systematic controls at the moment of loading. However, this shortcoming may negatively impact journeys starting from another Member State, where the suitability of the vehicles may not be systematically verified at the moment of loading as in the Netherlands.
