recommendations.text: Ensure that the sampling methodology for plant health checks provides for a sample which is representative, in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, in order to reasonably conclude that the consignment or lot is not contaminated with harmful organisms, in line with Article 13(1) of the same Directive.

citations.text: The work instructions include detailed provisions concerning the size of samples to be taken from lots of plants and plant products. The NVWA stated that the sampling methodology had been reviewed in light of recommendation 3 made in the previous audit report. The instructions for sampling of the main imported commodity types are summarised in Tables 2 to 4 below. Table 2: Extract of sampling instructions for plant health checks of cut flowers (source: NVWA, work instruction of 13-09-2017) Lot size (stems) Minimum sample size Unit of (number of units) per lot inspection <100 50% 400 ­ 10 000 200 10 001 ­ 25 000 300 25 001 ­ 40 000 400 40 001 ­ 55 000 500 50 001 ­ 70 000 600 Stems 70 001 ­ 85 000 700 85 001 ­ 100 000 800 100 001 ­ 125 000 900 125 001 ­ 150 000 1 000 150 001 ­ 200 000 1 100 >200 000 1 200 NOTE: the sample units must be collected from a minimum of two packages, and no more than 200 units can be collected from any single package Table 3: Extract of sampling instructions for plant health checks of fruits and vegetables (source: NVWA, work instruction of 13-09-2017) Lot size (packages) Minimum sample size Unit of (number of units) per lot inspection <100 2 100 ­ 300 3 301 - 500 3 501 ­ 1000 4 1001 ­ 2000 Packages 5 2001 ­ 3000 7 3001 ­ 4000 9 4001 - 5000 11 8 5001 ­ 6000 13 >6000 15 Table 4: Extract of sampling instructions for cuttings (source: NVWA, work instruction of 13- 09-2017) Lot size (pieces/genus) Minimum sample size Unit of (number of units) per lot inspection 1 - 200 50% 201 ­ 10 000 100 Pieces For each 10 000, or part thereof, additionally 100 Maximum 1 000 NOTE: No minimum number of packages is specified from which to select the sample units

Notwithstanding the size of the sample (in terms of the number of sample units), the audit team found that the number of packages from which samples are collected can be small in proportion to the total number of packages in a lot. The audit team observed inspections of fruits, cut flowers and cuttings, which were all sampled in line with the work instructions, and noted that: for seven lots of citrus, which contained between 1 500 and 1 780 packages, the sample was taken from five packages (since this is the unit of sampling); for one lot containing 110 packages of cut flowers of Solidago sp. the sample was collected from three packages; and for one lot containing 240 packages of cuttings of Euphorbia pulcherrima, the sample was taken from five packages.

Possible infestation in a lot or consignment may be unevenly distributed, whereby only the plants in an individual package are affected. Therefore, the small number of packages from which samples are taken, may not be sufficient in all cases to ensure that the sample can be considered representative of the lot, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

For cuttings, the sampling methodology has been revised since the previous audit, so that every genus in a consignment is considered as a separate lot and is subject to the same level of sampling (previously, for consignments containing more than one genus, up to six genera were subject to a standard intensity of sampling, and a lower intensity of sampling was applied to every other genus). In most cases, the sampling methodology provides an adequate level of statistical reliability, according to ISPM 31. However, for small lots (<10 000 pieces), the sampling methodology generally provides less than a 90% level of confidence of detecting a 2% level of infestation, according to ISPM 31.

In some cases, the sampling methodology provided in the official work instructions may not fully ensure that samples are representative with respect to their size or selection 9 Source: NVWA Annual phytosanitary report 2017 (https://www.nvwa.nl/documenten/plant/fytosanitair/fytosanitair/inspectieresultaten/rapport-fytosanitaire- signaleringen-2017) 11 from the lot or consignment. This limits the statistical reliability of the plant health checks carried out.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, with respect to sampling: Inspectors selected the sample for inspection themselves and were free from interference from third parties; Inspectors had access to the entire consignment and samples were collected from packages selected at random from different points of the consignment; The size of samples taken for inspection was in line with the work instructions (see section 5.1.4 above); The audit team observed four inspections of citrus fruits from South Africa. For one lot of Citrus paradisi, two boxes were selected for visual checks, each 20 containing 20 fruit and all the fruit in the boxes (40 in total) were inspected; for another lot of Citrus sinensis, five boxes were selected, two contained 56 fruit and three contained 22 fruit, all the fruit (178 in total) were inspected. Consequently, the inspections of these lots were not based on at least 200 fruit, which is not in line with Article 6 of Decision 2016/715. For each of the other two lots, 280 fruit were inspected in total from five boxes.

However, in line with the work instructions, inspections of citrus fruit covered by EU emergency measures against citrus black spot, are sometimes carried out on significantly fewer fruit than is required.

recommendations.text: Ensure that plant health checks consist of meticulous inspections of consignments or lots, in their entirety or on one or more representative samples, in line with Article 13a(1)(a) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, in order to reasonably conclude that the lot is not contaminated with harmful organisms, in line with Article 13(1) of the same Directive.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, with respect to the implementation of the checks: Inspectors had a good knowledge of the different harmful organisms which the commodities they were inspecting were most likely to host; The audit team observed three inspections of pomelo (Citrus maxima) from China, each fruit was individually wrapped in both clear plastic wrapping and red plastic netting. The inspector removed the wrapping from half of the fruit and carried out a thorough visual inspection of each fruit, cutting any fruit with suspect symptoms. The remaining fruit were not unwrapped, and the inspector carried out a visual inspection of the visible parts of the surface of the fruit. The inspection of the wrapped fruit could not be considered meticulous since much of the surface of the fruit was obscured by the wrapping materials. The inspector cited the section in the official work instructions which provided for the practice of only unwrapping 50% of the sampled units. The KCB stated that this practice was only common in the case of pomelo fruits from China, and less frequently for some consignments of blueberries (Vaccinium sp.) from South America; The audit team also observed inspections of bare root cuttings of Chrysanthemum indicum by inspectors from the Naktuinbouw, and of bare root cuttings of Euphorbia pulcherrima by inspectors of the KCB. Both checks were carried out consistently and in both cases inspectors identified whiteflies and leaf miners as harmful organisms of particular concern. The inspectors did not look at each stem (the sample unit) individually but rather looked at 50 cuttings simultaneously, checking all visible sides of the bunch of cuttings and making some effort to spread them out but not such that each cutting was separated and substantially visible; The checks of individually packaged fruit and cuttings were not considered by the audit team to be meticulous, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(a) of Directive 2000/29/EC. A similar point (recommendation No. 2), was also made in the previous audit report. All other checks observed were considered meticulous.
Plant health checks of cuttings and individually packaged fruit cannot be considered meticulous, and this reduces the efficacy of detecting any harmful organisms which may be present.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all interceptions are notified in accordance with Commission Directive 94/3/EC, in particular, interceptions made of plants, plant products and other objects imported in passengers' baggage or by post or courier, as required by Article 2 of the same Directive.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the notification procedures laid down in Commission Directive 94/3/EC are generally complied with. However, the NVWA do not notify interceptions related to passengers' baggage, postal or courier imports (see sections 5.3.5 and 5.3.4 above respectively), which is not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Directive 94/3/EC.

Interceptions involving passengers' baggage, postal and courier imports are not notified to the Commission and other Member States, including those involving the presence of harmful organisms or prohibited articles. This does not enable the Commission and other Member States to evaluate and potentially mitigate the risk posed by such imports.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the objectives set in the Multi-Annual National Control Plan, as required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 42, are relevant to, and can be measured by, the outcome of the controls. and

citations.text: The objectives for animal welfare in the 2015-2018 Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) include: a. To increase compliance, with a target of 80% compliance or better from the result of inspections. b. To include a random selection of farms for comparison of their compliance results with the risk chosen farms.

The report on the implementation of the MANCP in 2017 indicates that: a. For pigs, 350 production sites were inspected with an overall compliance rate of 70%. For calves the compliance rate was 60%, and the report concluded that this level of compliance was "moderate". For broilers, the compliance rate was 45% and the report concluded that this was unsatisfactory. b. The results do not give a representative picture of compliance within the sector as the inspections were conducted with other controls: for the purpose of cross compliance; for a project; in response to a notification from a third party. The report does not provide any indication of how the results from the inspections of the randomly selected farms compare with the results from the farms chosen on the basis of risk. 4 The MANCP network reference document "Developing Objectives and Indicators" states that the underlying principle behind these requirements and guidelines is that we cannot manage our control systems without setting clear objectives and monitoring progress towards those objectives. A strategic objective is a long- term objective, setting out what an official control system and its priorities intend to achieve. Strategic objectives usually relate to outcomes and impacts. Objectives should be Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-bound (SMART). 3

The NVWA does not measure whether the objective to increase compliance to 80% or better has been met(6). The reports on the implementation of the MANCP acknowledges that risk based checks increase the probability of finding non-compliant farms and results therefore do not demonstrate the overall level of compliance. The NVWA has not analysed the results from randomly selected farms to conclude whether this objective was met or not, or adjusted the objective so that it matches better to risk based controls.

recommendations.text: To apply the criteria for the cumulative daily mortality rate for broiler flocks as indicated in point 1(c) Annex V to this Directive when monitoring holdings with broiler chickens, as required by Directive 2007/43/EC Article 3(5). and

citations.text: In the broiler sector, Directive 2007/43/EC point 1(c) Annex V requires that in at least seven consecutive subsequently checked flocks from a house the cumulative daily mortality rate is below 1 % + 0,06 % multiplied by the slaughter age of the flock in days. However, NVWA guidance requires the cumulative daily mortality rate to be below 5%, which is higher than allowed by the Directive, e.g. for a flock with a slaughter age of 42 days the limit is 3.52%9. 8 http://www1.clermont.inra.fr/wq/index.php?id=protocol&prod 7

Animal based indicators are well established in the broiler sector, where the data is collected at slaughterhouses and used to select the highest risk farms for inspection. Although this is a robust system of control it does not make use of certain indicators which are required by EU legislation, i.e. verification of daily mortality rates and the limit for cumulative daily mortality rates for broiler flocks operating at the higher stocking densities.

recommendations.text: To ensure that information about the arrival of consignments of processed animal proteins is notified to the Member State of origin, by means of TRACES, as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, contrary to the requirements of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the NVWA does not systematically confirm the arrival of consignment of PAP to competent authorities of the Member State of origin by means of TRACES. The system of checks in place is based on random selection of certain consignments in TRACES and a cross-check of these data on the spot. Only 10% of required confirmations took place in recent years. The frequency of confirmation to the place of origin did however increase to 20% in 2019 (see also finding 20).

Inadequate implementation of EU requirements concerning transmission of information to the competent authority of the Member State of origin or destination via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP undermines the reliability of information on the intra- EU trade of such products.

responses.response: The NVWA prepares a new procedure to ensure that information about the arrival of consignments of processed animal proteins is fied to the Member State of origin, by means of TRACES, including extra employees for these (administrative) tasks.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the departure of consignments of organic fertilisers and soil improvers containing PAP are notified in TRACES as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: The competent authority stated that trade of consignments of OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM is not notified in TRACES. This is not in line with Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

Inadequate implementation of EU requirements concerning transmission of information to the competent authority of the Member State of origin or destination via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP undermines the reliability of information on the intra- EU trade of such products.

responses.response: The Dutch authorities disagrees with the finding and mmendation to notify OF/SI containing PAP consignments in intracommunity trade. We do not see any legal requirement in the ABP regulation to substantiate this recommendation. The wording of the article 48.3 of Regulation (EU) no. 1069/2009 clearly states that "PAP derived from category 3 material" needs a notification via TRACES by the MS of origin. There is no mention of "and products containing PAP" as is done in other parts of the Regulation when it is the intention of the legislator to include not 100% pure products. This interpretation is supported by the majority of MS as confirmed during the working group on ABP of 15 October 2018.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the seals of consignments of processed animal protein intended for export are checked at the point of exit from the EU, that the records of these checks are recorded in TRACES and that the competent authority responsible for the processing plant from which the consignment originated verifies that the seal checks have been carried out, as required by points 1(c) and (d), Section E, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

citations.text: Checks on exports of consignments of ruminant PAP via the port of Rotterdam are is carried out in accordance with the internal instructions of the NVWA. The competent authority stated that there are two types of official controls on exported consignments from the Netherlands, namely administrative and physical controls. Administrative checks on consignments with the origin in the Netherlands are carried out in the processing plants, including check of data in TRACES. Following the pre-notification via e-mail the local inspectors can carry out a random check of the containers at the point of exit. However, the audit team noted that the pre-notification via e-mail from the operator to the competent authority does not comply with the instruction from the NVWA as regards the content of such pre- notification. The audit team also noted that such checks do not ensure the check required at the point of exit as required in point 1 of section E of Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

Physical controls (seal checks) are carried out at an inspection centre of the BIP Rotterdam approved for import of liquid fats, oils and fish oils at Maastank B.V. No seal checks are carried out on consignments with origin in other Member States (Belgium, United Kingdom). This is not in line with point 1 of section E of Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. As regards consignments from Ireland, the competent authority stated that these consignments are only being transhipped in the port of Rotterdam.

The NVWA inspectors who do not have access to TRACES carry out seal checks on a certain proportion of consignments intended for export. There is no procedure in place to require that the competent authority responsible for the exit point (border inspection 10 post) informs via TRACES the competent authorities of the processing plants about the arrival of the consignment at the exit point and such notifications are not made by the inspectors. This is not in line with point (c) of section E of Chapter 5 of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

The lack of an adequate control mechanism in place to verify at the point of exit that all consignments of ruminant PAP exported from the Netherlands and other EU Member States have actually left the EU territory undermines the effectiveness of official controls in place.

recommendations.text: To ensure that microbiological sampling and record keeping of the 30 days validation of processing method 7 is in line with point G, Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) 142/2011.

citations.text: Three processing plants visited during the audit use processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant, during the 30 day validation period microbiological samples had been taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) by the operator. The audit team noted that the sampling frequency and laboratory results were in compliance with EU legislation.

In another processing plant visited, the validation report provided by the operator to the competent authority at the time of validation did not contain all of the processing 8 parameters required by point G 2, Chapter III, of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 142/2011. The competent authority had not noticed this shortcoming.

However, problems identified regarding operators' validation of method 7 in the 11 processing plants and the official assessments thereof, undermine confidence in the reliability of the results of official controls on this aspect of PAP production.

recommendations.text: The CA should introduce appropriate safeguard mechanisms to ensure that when private practitioners are appointed as OV they perform their duties without any conflict of interest in line with Article 5(1) of

citations.text: The CA informed the audit team that there is an internal procedure in place that foresees that the same private veterinary practitioner cannot certify the emergency slaughter and also perform the PMI of the same animal. Should a private veterinarian find themselves in this position they must report this to his/her supervisor and ask to be replaced. There are no safeguard measures in place to ensure that conflict of interest is avoided or to be able to verify that the above procedure is strictly followed.

In the case where the CA identifies that a private veterinarian is not acting in line with their entrusted official duties, then he/she can be excluded from future official assignments and a note is introduced in the Register. The CA also informed the audit team that they have requested private veterinarians to perform, if possible, their official duties in areas located outside the areas where they normally carry out their own private work. The CA does not verify if this request is followed. 5.2.3. Staffing and equipment

There are certain procedures in place ensuring that the OVs involved in private veterinary practice are impartial and free of conflict of interest. Nonetheless, there are no safeguard mechanisms or measures in place to verify that those procedures are adhered to.

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that when OAs carries out AMI under the responsibility of the OV this is fully in line with the requirements of Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624.

citations.text: The CA indicated to the audit team that in certain cases OAs can carry out AMI of poultry under the responsibility of the OV without meeting the requirements of Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. This Article specifies, among other requirements, that for the above to take place the AMI must be carried out previously by an OV in the holding of provenance.

Regarding the poultry slaughterhouses, the official controls, appear in line with the newly introduced EU requirements. Nonetheless, a number of OAs are allowed to carry out AMI under the responsibility of the OVs without meeting the conditions set in Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls cover the provisions of Article 10(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, namely that they are capable of consistent verification of feed business operators' fulfilment of obligations on appropriateness of retained samples taken, as required by the section on "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: Project protocols seen (see finding 11) contained adequate instructions for controls of retained samples (i.e. those to be taken and kept by FeBOs from ingredients and final products manufactured). The inspection reports assessed by the auditor contained satisfactory information on official controls of retained samples in FeBOs. Local feed inspectors interviewed demonstrated good knowledge on the practical implementation of such controls. However, the auditor noted, that in three out of five relevant establishments assessed this control was not adequately implemented, even though required by internal instructions. In the food-producing establishment, the feed inspector controlled the traceability of the produced feed materials. Checks on implementation of point 4 of Annex II "Quality Control" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 on collection and storage of retained samples was part of the project protocol, but it was overlooked during official control. Compliance of the operator with this legal requirement was also not checked by the food inspector.

The auditor assessed the report of the official control on the sole approved primary producer of feed. The feed inspector stated that requirements of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 were checked, but findings were not recorded in official reports. The auditor requested additional evidence (operator`s documentation on collection and storage of retained samples, results of tests of mixing homogeneity, and procedure on calibration of measuring devices) and the assessment of these documents from the local inspector. The competent authority provided adequate evidence; the assessment of the calibration of the measuring devices and test on homogeneity of mixing were satisfactory. The competent authority did not provide the operator`s documentation on collection and storage of retained samples. The collected retained 6 samples were clearly labelled and stored by the operator under conditions, which prevented adulteration. However, the samples were not sealed which contradicts the requirements of point 4 of Annex II "Quality Control" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

Inspections are planned in the form of risk-based project inspections and system audits, ensuring that the official controls are carried on a risk-basis. The inspectors' assessment of FeBOs' hazard analysis, results of tests on mixing homogeneity and carry-over, verification of implementation of traceability requirements were largely adequate. However, the effectiveness of feed inspections is weakened by shortcomings in officials' verification of the correctness of feed labelling and inconsistent verification of collection and storage of retained samples. 7 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls cover the provisions of Article 10(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, namely that they are capable of verifying that feed business operators' labelling satisfies the requirements laid down in Articles 15, 16 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 and Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003.

citations.text: In general, verification of whether operators meet the legislative labelling requirements is part of the system audits (see finding 12). In addition, one specific project was also carried out on labelling (see finding 11). During the interviews, the auditor reviewed with the local inspectors several labels of the FeBOs included in the programme. While the inspectors interviewed demonstrated in general good knowledge of the subject, in several cases the inspectors did not identify certain inaccuracies/non-compliances: The identification codes of feed additives were missing on labels of feed additives, contrary to Article 16(1)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Technological feed additives with maximum limits were not labelled on premixtures which is a legal requirement in Article 16(1)(a) and (f) of, and Annex III to, Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Absence of declaration of feed materials on the label, contrary to Article 16(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. Based on a dosage instruction of a complementary feed, the daily intake of a feed additive was lower than the minimum required in the authorisation of the additive by Regulation (EC) No 885/2010. Declarations on type of feed (complete, complementary, etc.) were not in line with the legal requirements of Article 15(a) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. Dosage instruction for complementary feed (dairy cow) was not on the label, contrary to Article 17(b) and point 4 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009.

Inspections are planned in the form of risk-based project inspections and system audits, ensuring that the official controls are carried on a risk-basis. The inspectors' assessment of FeBOs' hazard analysis, results of tests on mixing homogeneity and carry-over, verification of implementation of traceability requirements were largely adequate. However, the effectiveness of feed inspections is weakened by shortcomings in officials' verification of the correctness of feed labelling and inconsistent verification of collection and storage of retained samples. 7 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: Ensure that import consignments of specified seeds are sampled in accordance with provisions of Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191 taking into consideration the associated plant health risk, as required by Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The NVWA stated that coated tomato and pepper seeds are excluded from the sampling regime as coating may affect the tests. In particular, chemicals in the coating could influence the RNA extraction or inhibit the PCR process. Currently there are no validated laboratory protocols for coated seeds. The majority of the seeds are imported as minimally processed. The growers use chemicals during the extraction and dry the seeds before the dispatch.

Consignments or seed lots of Capsicum spp., for which the AD on the PC certifies that the variety is resistant, are accepted for import. NVWA stated that there are uncertainties about which genes ensure the resistance. During their monitoring activity for ToBRFV the NVWA tested positive pepper seed lots, which had been declared to be ToBRFV resistant. Resistance of a variety could be linked to only one of the two parental lines. Hence, a contamination of the hybrid seed may only be related to the parents whereas the seed itself is still resistant.

At the time of the audit, the inspection bodies selected consignments for sampling randomly, without taking into consideration the existing risk such as countries, exporters and varieties with ToBRFV interception history. The NVWA is of the opinion that ToBRFV is much wider distributed in the world than officially recorded. Therefore, 21 third countries were evenly targeted, to avoid overlooking potential risky pathways. The audit team considers that a non-targeted sampling reduces the effectiveness of the test in preventing the entry of infected seed lots to the EU territory. In addition, the audit team noted that the IT system run by the two inspection bodies does not enable the NVWA to check real-time, whether the mandatory sampling rate set by Regulation (EU) 2020/1191 is observed. The CAs stated that the ongoing upgrade of the IT system and the database in which the import inspections are registered would enable the inspectors to take into consideration risk criteria for the selection of consignments for sampling. The upgraded system is expected to be operational in the course of 2021.

The controls of imported seeds are generally in line with EU requirements. However, the selection of consignments for laboratory tests does not take into consideration all known risk factors and no measures are implemented to prevent the free circulation of imported seeds before the laboratory analysis is completed. These issues compromise the effectiveness of EU measures to protect against the introduction of ToBRFV in seeds.

citations.text: If the consignment was sampled, the importer receives a notification about the sampled lot. The company is then informed about the test results in writing. The audit team noted that at the time of the audit no official measures were applied to block the consignment until the laboratory test was completed, although Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191 requires laboratory tests due to the existing plant health risk. Therefore, the exemption provided by Article 4(9) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130 does not apply and the consignments cannot be released for free circulation before the test results are available. The approach followed by the CAs meant that some seed lots were placed on the market before the laboratory analysis was completed, including at least one documented case, where the sample tested positive for ToBRFV. The NVWA stated that the relevant instructions will be amended and the consignments will be blocked until the tests are finalised. recommendations.text: To ensure that at primary production of food of non-animal origin, competent authorities perform official controls on microbiological risks on a risk basis as required by Article 1(2)(a) in conjunction with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: For audits, if the FBO has a Private Quality Assurance Scheme (PQS) certified according to BRC, IFS, FSSC 22000, the frequency of audits could be reduced. Audits do not apply to primary production and having a PQS is not taken into account for reducing the frequency of official controls at this stage. Details are in the following table. Table: Official Controls frequency over FBOs in the scope of this audit. FNAO FBOs AUDIT'S FREQUENCY INSPECTION'S FREQUENCY PQS PRIMARY PRODUCTION Not established N/A Carried out by Projects SPROUT-PRODUCING ESTABLISHMENT PROCESSOR 1 every 1 every 1 every Freezing and/or Cutting Plants 3 years 6 years year Fruit and Vegetables 1 every To be Not yet fixed 5 years established Based on the CAs capacity
In primary production, controls are in the form of special projects, that take place with the aim of obtaining information on the whole sector regarding microbiological risks of produce.

For these "special projects", each year, a crop category is identified and a limited number of FBOs is randomly selected (see table in paragraph 61) for microbiological inspections. Regardless of the outcome of the project, a different category is chosen for the following year, without continuity and without having a plan of when the FBO / category will be inspected further (see table in paragraph 54).

The prioritisation of these projects and controls is mainly based on the risks associated with pesticides and, to a minor extent, the risks of microbial contamination (i.e. EFSA opinion regarding crops posing particular risks).

The inspectors interviewed stated that a better balance between chemical and microbiological risks in prioritising official controls is advisable and it should be reflected in the official control risk-based plan. The inspectors informed the audit team that controls over hygiene at primary production is still a relatively new task.

The CCA informed the audit team that the approach in place aims to optimise the resources available. However, the team leader of the primary production area acknowledged that, based on the current state of implementation of projects, it is more likely to identify systematic deficiencies and to improve the sector for pesticides, whereas this is not possible for microbiological risks. The CCA informed the audit team that: a) in 2017, for this project, 80% of implementation. Half of the inspected PP were PQS certified and there were no significant differences in the outcome of the inspections; b) in 2018, implementation stopped at 60% mainly due to other priorities related to official controls and difficulties in having the selected FBO with the targeted crop at the time of the inspection; c) in 2019, only 19 crops posing particular risks out of 69 inspected fell within the scope of this audit (implementation drop to 19%), mainly due to difficulties in having the selected FBO with the targeted crop at the time of the inspection; d) in 2020, no inspections were carried out due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

In primary production, the system of official controls covers both chemical (PPP) and microbiological risks, with greater attention being given to the former. As a result, the likelihood of detecting non-compliances with microbiological requirements is lower. In addition, non-compliances detected during the controls are not considered for future planning. This could lead to associated food safety risks being underestimated, weakening the system of official controls and thus the enforcement of EU legislation in this area. 5.2.4 Implementation of official controls over FBO obligations Legal requirements Articles 9(1)(d), 14 and 44(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 4 to 8, and Annexes I and II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 208/2013, Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/628, Article 1 and Annex I to Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

The inspectors interviewed confirmed to the audit team that official controls are implemented at the primary producers in the scope of the specific project. However, the driving force to perform inspections is still pesticides residues; microbiological risks could also be part of the inspections.

Inspectors informed the audit team that due to time constraints the specific checklist (see paragraph 63) is not used systematically. The assessments of hygiene requirements can also differ, depending on the experience and on the knowledge that an inspector may have of an FBO. Thus, official controls are not systematically carried out in a coherent and uniform way, so are not effectively targeting microbiological risks.

When non-compliances were identified, corrective actions were systematically required but evidence of follow-up was not systematically available. Moreover, inspectors confirmed that non-compliances are not yet taken into account for future planning.

Generally, checklists were not part of the reports and were not stored / archived. Therefore, the traceability of the official controls depended on what was noted in the report, where usually, only non-compliances were recorded. Aspects related to PPP were well described and supported by solid evidence in the reports, which was not the case for microbiological risks related issues. Sprout-producing establishments

Regarding primary production, official controls are not consistently implemented. When implemented, the official controls partially targeted microbiological risks and are focusing mainly on chemical risks (PPP). This is not in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In addition, the specific checklist for microbiological inspections at primary production is not systematically used and when used not always documented, thus official controls are not carried out in a coherent and uniform way and are not effectively targeting microbiological risks.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls verify the certification requirements for imports into the EU of seeds intended for the production of sprouts, as required by Regulation (EU) 2019/628.

citations.text: Regarding controls at sprout-producing establishments, the checklists used were the same as those used for processors of FNAO (which are also the same as those used for food of animal origin). Not all elements related to the specific legislation for sprouts were included 17 (i.e. import certificate requirements are not indicated). The inspectors confirmed that such a generic checklist could not provide guidance to inspectors during official controls at sprout-producing establishments.

In the reports examined by the audit team, as well as in the summary of non-compliances provided by the CCA, there was no evidence of non-compliances having been identified during official controls related to import certificates of seeds for sprouting.

When reviewing the outcome of official controls of sprout-producing establishments, the audit team noted that evidence of what was checked during official controls, regarding import certificates of seeds for sprouting imported from third countries, was rarely traceable.

The inspectors confirmed that the generic checklist that was in use up until the end of 2020, made it difficult to provide evidence of official controls over import certificates of seeds for sprouting controls.

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that a specific checklist is now in place (since the start of 2021), which includes all of the specific requirements of the EU legislation for sprouts and seeds for sprouting. This checklist was assessed as satisfactory by the audit team.

However, shortcomings in the use of this new checklist were observed, mainly related to the fact that inspectors limited the assessment of compliance to the import certificates requirement based on the statement of FBOs, instead of seeking evidence (i.e. presence of the import certificate).

In one case, the audit team observed that the import certificate requirements for mung bean had been assessed as satisfactory without having had the certificate available. The team leader inspector (CA) informed the audit team that this was his usual method, but in the 18 future he will ensure to check for the physical presence of the certificate and its compliance with EU legislation.
Furthermore, at the request of the audit team, the CA requested the certificate from the operator. The operator was unable to provide it by the end of this audit.

Whilst the official controls relating to sprout-producing establishments identify regularly non compliances and did not adequately cover the legal requirements of import certificate for seeds from third countries, which could result in contaminated product being placed on the market.

The CA has procedures, instructions and checklists that enable the CAs to perform official controls of FNAO establishments and for establishments seeking approval, in a uniform fashion. However, the generic checklists in use up until the end of 2020 for sprout-producing establishments, in conjunction with the fact that in primary production the checklist was not systematically used, prevent inspectors from carrying out official controls in a consistent manner.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authorities have procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and other official activities, as required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The CCA informed the audit team that supervision activities of inspectors, including on- the-spot visit of FBOs, could be carried out yearly by a senior inspector (team leader) if the capacity allows. However, there are no procedures or instructions in place for these supervisory activities. In addition, no records are kept of these activities so there is no evidence available of whether results are taken into account or how they are used in order to improve the system of official controls.

The CCA acknowledge that an effective system of verification on-the-spot of the implementation of training, procedures, instructions and use of checklists could improve the entire system of official controls. For example, if such a mechanism of supervision was in place, the CCA could have identified deficiencies in the controls of import 8 certificate requirements (see paragraphs 88, 93, 95 and 96) and consistency in the use of specific checklists during official controls on primary production (see paragraph 84), and could have corrected them in a timely manner.

The fact that the system of supervision in place does not include documented on-site verifications of inspectors affects the CAs' capability to assess the appropriateness and consistency of inspections, and to identify any shortcomings in their performance. 5.2.2 Registration/approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings Registration of primary producers of FNAO

However, shortcomings in the use of checklists at primary production and at sprout- producing establishments were observed by the audit team. These deficiencies were identified by the audit team and brought to the attention of the CCA which acknowledged 23 that the current procedures in place for supervision (overseeing of inspections), which are based only on desk studies and training activities, do not allow for the identification of such shortcomings (see paragraphs 29, 30, 31, 32 and 34).

recommendations.text: To ensure that the delegation granted to the veterinarians affiliated to SGD to carry out hygiene checks at milk and colostrum production holdings is withdrawn, as private veterinarians are not suitably qualified and experienced as required by Article 30(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The CAs responsible for the official control system over the production of milk and dairy products are clearly designated and their structure and organisation are adequate for the performance of their tasks. An exception, requiring legislative amendments, is the delegation given to private veterinarians to perform official controls in dairy holdings related to hygiene, for whom no provisions are in place to exclude potential conflicts of interest.

responses.response: In the designation Decree that the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport had initially published in December 2019, the veterinarians were designated for the provisions of Article 49 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Paragraph 4 of that article states the checks in the field of hygiene measures during, among other things, refrigerated storage, transport and processing. These are tasks that COKZ performs. The auditors therefore rightly concluded that there was an overlap between the tasks of the designated veterinarian and the COKZ and, moreover, that the private veterinarians are also not qualified for these checks. This omission has since been remedied because the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport has officially published a revised designation Decree in the Staatscourant of 12 November, 2021. In this revised designation Decree, the veterinarians are only designated for the activities under Article 49, paragraphs 1 and 3. Link to designation Decree: https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/stcrt-2021- 46139.html

citations.text: Following an application for approval, the COKZ registers the undertaking and starts the approval procedure. An initial on-site assessment is performed by COKZ personnel, 8 following which a conditional approval may be granted for 3 months; an extension of the conditional approval for further 3 months may be considered if significant progress has been made in meeting the requirements, but shortcomings have still been identified. The decision on approval is made by COKZ on behalf of the Minister of the VWS. In some cases (i.e. registered processors seeking approval, when processes and documentation are already well established) a final approval can be granted immediately. Approved FBOs are entered in the Synergy database, managed by COKZ, which contains contact details and other basic information of FBOs; only the FBOs inspected by COKZ are identified as such in Synergy. COKZ updates these lists around every three months. The CCA stated that at least twice a year there is a NVWA-COKZ consultation/meeting regarding the update of these lists. However, not all FBOs are inspected annually, and not all items relevant for verifying compliance with regulatory requirements are checked during an inspection. This shortcoming was also identified by NVWA audits of COKZ in 2018 and 2020 (see paragraph 105).

The approvals are granted for generic dairy processing activity. The lack of additional information on the type of products manufactured and processing makes the CAs verification of possible changes that may have occurred, regarding e.g. the equipment and production lines, challenging, although such changes might require approval by the CA (see paragraph 29). And while COKZ stated that inspection reports identify processes and products manufactured, these were not always clearly identified in the reports seen by the audit team: the inspection reports and Sinergy record activities and product groups.

COKZ stated that in case of changes in location or ownership, as well as when major changes in structures, equipment and products occur, the approval must be revised and possibly amended. When reviewing some approval files, the audit team noted that this systematic approach had not been consistently adhered to. Several FBOs had not timely informed COKZ about relevant changes, either planned or implemented. These changes were only assessed at the time of the following routine inspection. In such cases, no supporting documentation was available in order to demonstrate that the approval file had been scrutinised before granting the approval (i.e. updated blueprints, descriptions of modified equipment, production lines, procedures, etc.).

Nearly all raw milk in the country is collected by 36 operators, which were all registered by the COKZ until 2020. In 2020, the COKZ requested such operators with storage facilities to apply for approval as milk collection centres, in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Four FBOs applied, of which one was approved in 2020, one received a conditional approval in September 2021 and one is still active without an approval. The fourth contacted operator did not need a specific approval because it is using the storage facilities of another operator.

One of the milk collection centres moved to new premises in 2021 and had applied for an approval, which was granted one month after the inspection by the COKZ official as a final approval. No information was collected by COKZ to ascertain that no activities related to storage of milk had been carried out in the interim period, taking into account the same activity carried out by the FBO at its previous location (collection and storage of raw milk to deliver milk in specific quantities and quality according to client specifications).

The audit team noted that the validity of conditional approval is generally extended to the maximum of 6 months without a follow-up inspection being carried out at the end of the first 3-month period, as required by Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In some cases, the conditional approval of the FBO was retained for more than 6 months (in one case for 18 months).

Visits by COKZ inspectors on FBOs seeking approval were documented. However, the inspection reports did not mention this specific scope of the inspection, nor the final assessment of the inspector in relation to the approval.

The implementation of the system in place for approval of FBOs does not provide guarantees that all food businesses eligible for/requiring approval are provided with a valid approval, that the activities carried out are correctly covered by the approval, nor 10 that FBOs comply in full with regulatory requirements. In addition, no documented evidence was available as proof of a regular review of approvals.

citations.text: In case of non-compliances graded C, a warning is issued, referring to the deadlines for their correction as indicated in the inspection report. The audit team noted that the cover letters accompanying the written warnings and inspection reports delivered to the FBOs were sometimes issued up to 3 months following the inspection, when the deadlines agreed with the FBO at the time of the inspection for corrective actions had already elapsed. Follow-up on-site verifications were generally carried out at the time of the next planned inspection, without taking into account the deadlines previously agreed. No documentation on corrective actions planned or implemented by the FBOs was requested by the inspectors to enable an administrative/documentary follow-up, in cases where it was not possible to carry out an on-the-spot verification. This has been a systemic deficiency in the COKZ control system, which was also detected at the time of the NVWA audits in 2018 and 2020 (see paragraph 105).

The audit team noted that the inspectors used mostly D categorisation of non-compliances (minor shortcomings), although in some cases seen the shortcomings should have been categorised as C. For instance, in one case the FBO did not have a procedure in place to verify the effectiveness of the heat treatment and did not carry out any testing for alkaline phosphatase or microbiology in final products; this was considered as a D non- compliance. As a consequence of this categorisation, no follow-up visit was carried out 17 within the next 3 months to ensure the shortcoming had been rectified. In another case, a shortcoming was categorised twice as C (serious), however it should have already been escalated as it was a repeated non-compliance.

The audit team screened the reports of several FBOs and noted delays, sometimes significant and up to 3 months from the date of the inspection, in the delivery of reports and written warnings. This shortcoming had also been noted at the time of the NVWA audit on COKZ in 2018, and led to a specific recommendation (see paragraph 105). 5.6.2 Official controls at establishment level

The system of official controls covers the entire dairy sector and is based on procedures and instructions aimed at ensuring consistency and uniformity of official controls. However, the assurance that that operators comply with national and EU provisions, and that non-compliances are timely corrected and appropriately followed-up is undermined by the delays in their implementation.

An exception, requiring legislative amendments, is the delegation given to private veterinarians to perform official controls in dairy holdings related to hygiene, for whom no provisions are in place to exclude potential conflicts of interest.

responses.response: The veterinarians affiliated to SGD play a key role in ensuring that only milk from healthy animals is supplied. The independence of veterinarians is an important point of attention in the law and official regulations and in the other regulations by which the activities of veterinarians are safeguarded in practice. Assurance that veterinarians act free of conflict of interest in the performance of their official duties is therefore guaranteed by a combination of measures: 1. A veterinarian may only practice veterinary medicine if he/she is registered in the veterinary medicine register (Article 4.3 of the Animals Act). Independence of these veterinarians is guaranteed by the fact that they have a duty of care as included in Animals Act. Veterinarians can be held liable for non-compliance with this duty of care by way of disciplinary law. 2. Affiliation of veterinarians to an independent private assurance system, like SGD, also contributes to their independent position. recommendations.text: To ensure that NVWA undertakes a proper follow-up of its audits on COKZ and to close the outstanding recommendations only when the actions to remedy the shortcomings identified have been appropriate and fully implemented, as required in Article 33 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The NVWA performs annual audits at COKZ to test the performance of the delegated tasks, in line with the requirements of Article 33(a) of the OCR; this is also laid down in the Working Agreement between NVWA and COKZ. Three NVWA audits to COKZ were carried out in the period 2018-2020: the audits in 2018 and 2019 have been completed, whilst the 2020 audit was performed as a remote assessment of the follow-up of audit recommendations made in the 2018 and 2019 reports, due to the restrictions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The report of 2018 made 16 recommendations to COKZ, among which the following are considered relevant for the sector being audited: · re-inspections to be timely carried out in cases of non-compliances; · in case of serious infringements, identification of the correct legal basis should be included in the inspection report. The 2019 report followed-up the recommendations and guidance of the 2018 audit, and concluded that several recommendations had not been adequately addressed (including those mentioned above), and made the following additional recommendations: 24 · documentation on traceability to be checked during inspections; · sampling procedures to be brought in line with those of the national legislation, with inspectors being trained on these procedures; · temperature monitoring equipment for transport being checked for operation, use and maintenance. The 2020 report concluded that 25 out of the 27 recommendations of the 2019 report were addressed satisfactorily, with the exception of the following two: · recommendations from the NVWA audit report should be adequately addressed within reasonable deadlines; · to extend sampling to cases of non-compliances in accordance with existing procedures.

The audit team noted that the conclusions of the follow-up of the previous NVWA audits were in contrast with the finding of the DG Health and Food Safety audit as the recommendations of the previous NVWA audits were although the effectiveness of the measures adopted by COKZ had not been fully comprehensive. Moreover, serious non- compliances with regard to approval procedures were not taken into account.

Audits on delegated authorities are performed regularly, although not sufficiently in identifying all relevant shortcomings and enforcing the correction of the ones identified, as the recommendations of the audit reports had not or not comprehensively been addressed and followed-up.

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that when issuing health certificates for Intra- Community trade, to accompany live poultry for slaughter in another Member State, it uses the information available to the official controls to accurately reflect the Salmonella monitoring test results, in line with the required by Article 88, 3(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. to 68.

citations.text: In 2019, a turkey holding that had a positive test result in one house had tested twice more all houses, prior to sending them to slaughter, with those subsequent tests giving negative results. The operator informed that: All the Salmonella test results were sent to the slaughterhouse; and that the turkeys from the house with the initial positive result had been correctly registered as Salmonella positive in the food chain information form, even with two subsequent negative results.

The gap in the NVWA certification system concerning the Salmonella status of a flock had little to no impact in the possible spread of Salmonella. This due to the very low number of incorrect certificates and the correct reporting in the food chain information.

responses.response: From July 2021, the official veterinarians who issue health ertificates for Intra-Community trade will check the Salmonella ols status of a flock, based on the Salmonella monitoring test results with that are registered in the database KIPnet. This check ensures that the information of the official Salmonella controls is used when issuing certificates, in compliance with Article 88, 3 (C) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. After summer another check will be added to ensure that the accurate Salmonella monitoring test results are used for the certification. During the pre-screening of the export applications, the Salmonella monitoring test results of the flock will be directly consulted in the database KIPnet. On the day of certification the official veterinarians will do a second check on the accurate Salmonella status of the flocks, based on the Salmonella monitoring test results.

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that in laying hen flocks restrictive measures are taken on eggs originating from flocks already when suspected of being infected with relevant Salmonella serotypes in order to comply with Part D (2), Annex II to first bullet point.

citations.text: The audit team saw documented evidence of both NVWA and COKZ activities demonstrating that those are in line with EU requirements with two exceptions: 15 The national legislation and SNCP related instructions only require the NVWA to impose restrictive measures (in particular a ban on marketing of eggs) after confirmation of targeted Salmonella serovars. Therefore, a ban on the marketing of eggs is not imposed during the period when the positive Salmonella spp. results are already available and the flock should be considered suspect of being infected. This is not in line with Part D 2. of Annex II to Regulation 2160/2003. The timeframe between date of sampling and the date of reception of positive result for a targeted Salmonella serovar can range from 4-5 to 14 days which, depending on the size of the infected flock(s), can correspond to a few thousand eggs or as much as several hundred thousand; which is compounded by the fact that COKZ imposes restrictive measures on the eggs at holdings from the date of the test result of the targeted Salmonella serovar instead of from the date of the sampling. This meant that any eggs laid after the date of sampling and until the date of the test result were not blocked, nor recalled, from the market and could be sold as Class A eggs. This is not in line with Part D 2. of Annex II to Regulation 2160/2003.

The system in place provides guarantees that correct measures are taken when a laying hen flock is positive for a targeted Salmonella serovar. Measures taken on eggs after positive results are in general acceptable, but adopted with unnecessary delay (after serotyping). Additionally, the lack of clarity in one aspect of the delegation of control tasks to COKZ meant that there are no restrictions to placing on the market possibly contaminated eggs produced between the date of sampling and the date of reception of positive results, nor is recalling imposed. Therefore, the risk of Salmonella being spread from eggs to consumers is not fully mitigated. 17

responses.response: re Poultry farmers and laboratories will be obliged to report the detection of Salmonella spp. by automatic alert in the database KIPnet shortly. In the meantime notification will be done by email to the NVWA. In response the flock is declared suspected from the moment the samples were taken and all eggs produced thereafter, including those at the packing station, are blocked. If no target serotype is found, there is no longer a suspicion as mentioned in Part D (2), Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003 and the restrictions will be lifted. If a target serotype is found, the flock is declared infected and measures will be applied in line with Part D (2 and 3), Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that the audits or inspections, required by Article 33(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, that it performs on delegated bodies verify the correct understanding and performance of all delegated control tasks.

citations.text: From 2017 to 2019, the NVWA performed annual audits on COZK controls over laying hen holdings, and establishments further along in the egg production and marketing chain. The audits included accompanying a few COKZ inspections on the spot at each of those establishments. None of the audits detected deficiencies with COKZ performance in relation to the tasks delegated by the NVWA. 19

The NVWA audits did not look into how COKZ performed the egg channelling after the imposition of restriction measures in laying hen holdings. NVWA did not detect that COKZ was imposing restrictions on the eggs, and/or recalling those eggs, only from the date of the positive test result instead of from the date of the sampling for that test. Conclusions on official controls, verification and audits

The NVWA controls on delegated bodies have effectively ensured compliance from C-Mark. It did not detect that COKZ has been imposing restrictions on egg marketing later than required which indicates weaknesses in the effectiveness of NVWA controls over this body.

responses.response: cle The NVWA will perform an audit, as mentioned in Article 33(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, on COKZ in September 2021. audits.title: Official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that documented procedures for the performance of official controls are in place, and that they are updated as appropriate and implemented accordingly.

citations.text: The NVWA has issued documented procedures for performing official controls on consignments of animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU through Dutch BCPs, which include an import inspection manual (Werkhandboek Importkeuring) and instructions on the use of the electronic national veterinary border control system of the NVWA (Veterinaire Grens Controle Systeem ­ VGC system). The audit team noted that procedures are incomplete or are not in line with relevant EU requirements regarding transit (see section 5.2.3), internal audits, control verification procedures (see section 5.1.6) and identity checks on consignments of bulk liquid oils and fats (see section 5.2.4.2), which is not in line with Article 12(1) and (3) of the OCR. The manual and the majority of the documented procedures are publicly available. The 6 NVWA also maintains an online information system (Import Veterinair Online) for use by both NVWA staff and operators on the specific requirements for animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU.

The audit team noted that the procedure for the performance of documentary checks on goods of non-animal origin (K-IK-INV-PR03) was not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The procedure provides that, for products listed in Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793, the documentary check (see also sections 5.1.5 and 5.2.4) is solely for the verification of the completeness of part I of the Common Health Entry Document (CHED-D); there is no cross-check to see if the information in the CHED-D corresponds with that provided in official certificates, official attestations or other documents accompanying the consignment. In addition, the procedure provides that for products listed in Annex II to that Regulation, the documentary checks are performed on copies of official certificates and not on the originals (see also sections 5.1.5 and 5.2.4). The audit team further noted that there are no arrangements to take corrective actions if the mandatory frequencies specified in EU law for identity and physical checks on food of non-animal origin are not met (see also section 5.2.4).

The Commission audit team noted that during the ABB audits of compliance of the inspection centres and control points with minimum requirements, and the ABB verification controls at BCPs, the ABB auditors had not identified several of the non- compliances identified by the Commission team, some of which were significant (see finding 68). The ABB reports evaluated by the Commission team neither contained deadlines by which non-compliances were to be remedied nor requests for action plans to be submitted.

Furthermore, the Commission audit team noted that the findings in the ABB reports had been poorly communicated to the import control team and there was little evidence that the shortcomings identified had been followed-up by the import control team. The Commission audit team also observed that most of the non-compliances were repeatedly found in subsequent audit or verification control reports. Most of the NVWA staff interviewed stated that they were unaware of the reported non-compliances and had no access to the ABB reports recorded in the NVWA database.

The audit team found that the failure by the NVWA to take appropriate measures in the light of the results of its internal audits or corrective actions in all cases where its control verification procedures identified shortcomings was not in line with Article 6(1) and 12(3) of the OCR respectively.

Whilst official controls on animals and goods entering the EU are conducted by appropriately trained staff and underpinned by documented procedures and comprehensive information technology systems, verification of consistent application of controls and compliance of facilities is weak. This is compounded by an ineffective internal audit and control verification system which either did not identify shortcomings or, if they were identified, did not follow-up on the timely rectification of these shortcomings. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

The audit team identified that for three consignments of animal origin which were split during transit, the traceability of those consignments was not ensured: · For one non-conforming consignment of over 100 000 kg fish, the CHED issued on arrival at the BCP indicated that the consignment arrived in bulk by vessel. Before the consignment was transported to a free warehouse, a second CHED had been issued at the BCP indicating that the consignment had arrived at the BCP in one container with a fictitious container number and 12 seals. The NVWA clarified that the consignment was transported from the BCP to the free warehouse in 12 road trips. The original consignment in transit was therefore split before it reached its destination, which is not in line with Article 19(e) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. In addition, traceability of this non-conforming consignment could not be guaranteed. · A second consignment was split into several consignments after storage in a customs warehouse. However, the sum of quantities declared in the split CHEDs exceeded the quantities in the original CHED, which is not in line with Article 28(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. Consequently, the competent authority did not ensure through its verification that the traceability system in place at the warehouse was effective, which is not in line with Article 26(2) of said Regulation. · A third consignment, according to the health certificate, originated from two establishments in a third country. The original CHED and subsequent split CHEDs issued after storage indicated one establishment of origin only. The overall quantity in the split CHEDs for one establishment of origin exceeded the quantities mentioned on the health certificate, which is not in line with Article 28(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. Consequently, the competent authority did not ensure through its verification that the traceability system in place at this warehouse was effective, which is not in line with Article 26(2) of said Regulation. 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks of consignments

The audit team noted that the identity checks on consignments of bulk liquid oils arriving in vessels were performed either (a) on the basis of a seal check in the absence of an (14) https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/3853 13 official seal, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, or (b) a full identity check. The NVWA stated that it does not verify the quantity of bulk liquid oils when performing identity checks. This is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The audit team also observed that in this respect, the NVWA's procedures do not require verification of the quantity of consignments of bulk liquids. 5.2.4.3 Checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin

The NVWA stated that documentary checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin, when not selected by the VGC system for identity and physical checks, are performed automatically by the VGC system based on the completeness of the information contained in part I of the CHED-D, and without taking into account the information contained in official certificates, attestations or other documents accompanying the consignment. This is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

The NVWA further confirmed that documentary checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin which are selected for identity and physical checks are performed on scanned copies of official certificates, attestations or other documents accompanying the consignment rather than on the original documents. This is also not in line with Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.
Consequently, the previous recommendation made in audit report DG(SANTE) 2017- 6054 regarding the performance of documentary checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin remains unaddressed.

Whilst consignments of animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU are presented for official controls, and said controls are carried out in line with documented arrangements, some are not performed in line with EU rules (e.g. documentary checks are not performed at the BCP of entry in all cases) and a long-standing shortcoming concerning controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit remains. Regarding goods of non-animal origin, systematic, and in some cases long-standing shortcomings in the implementation of those controls remain, notably concerning the performance of documentary checks, the locations at which those checks are performed and the frequencies at which identity and physical checks are performed. The fact that the competent authorities have not ensured the implementation of official controls in line with EU rules undermines assurances that goods of non-animal origin entering the EU through Dutch BCPs comply with applicable requirements.

The audit team found that two of the 14 inspection centres visited were compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs. The other 12 inspection centres and the two control points visited were not compliant with the requirements laid down in Articles 64(3) and 53(1)(a) of the OCR respectively and Articles 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. Many of the shortcomings identified by the audit team (and listed in findings 69 and 70) had not been identified by the ABB in its internal audit and control verification activities (see finding 31).

The fact that the majority of BCPs, including their inspection centres, and control points visited were not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin for which they had been designated demonstrates a systematic failure in the competent authority's internal audit and control verification system and compromises the ability of the competent authority to provide assurances that animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU through Dutch BCPs are appropriately handled, processed and stored and that only compliant animals and goods enter the EU.

audits.title: assess the controls on Antimicrobial Veterinary Medicinal Products

recommendations.text: To ensure that all antimicrobials are used in accordance with the terms of their marketing authorisations, as required by Article 106(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/6.

citations.text: The competent authorities declared their view that the marketing authorisations for certain old antimicrobials are no longer in line with the most recent scientific knowledge, in that they often indicate doses that are too low and are administered for periods that are too long.

For old antimicrobials and for specific cases laid down in the prescription guidelines for the veterinary profession, the competent authorities allow veterinarians to deviate, the dose and duration of the treatment, from the terms of the corresponding marketing authorisations. The competent authorities declared that their goal is that when decisions for such a deviation are taken by veterinarians, these are based on scientific knowledge, and always follow a consistent approach. In order to do that, the guidelines detail the extent of deviation allowed for each condition, antimicrobial and animal species. It follows that there are not official controls to verify that these old antimicrobials are used in accordance with the terms of their marketing authorisations, as laid down in Article 106(1) of the VMPR.

The planning and implementation of veterinary controls that the NVWA carries out is appropriate to verify compliance with most of the requirements of the VMPR under the scope of this audit, and therefore largely contributes to a more prudent use of antimicrobials. However, the NVWA allow veterinarians to use old antimicrobials outside of the terms of their marketing authorisation.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the system in place can ensure that sampling at border control posts is fully representative as required by Article 3(1) of and Annex (point 3.3 of Part A) to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729.

citations.text: Regarding sampling at BCPs: i. Seven BCPs are designated for products of animal origin although approximately 90% of fresh meat arrives via Rotterdam port. Schiphol, and to a lesser extent, Eemshaven are the only other BCPs that have received imported fresh meat over the past four years. ii. The selection of eligible consignments for sampling is done by the Veterinary Border Control system based on: · the list of CN codes for fresh meat, as discussed during the drafting of the EU Decision, and · the list of BCPs and origins included in the TRACES data from year -2 and first half of year -1 (data used for preparing the sampling plan). iii. The audit team identified consignments from a few origins that were not sampled in 2021. The competent authority confirmed that the current system only flags consignments from origins and/or BCPs identified in the sampling plan instead of all CN codes for all origins and all BCPs approved for fresh meat. This means that some consignments may not be identified for sampling, which is not in line with point 3.3(a) of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. iv. The correct sampling rates were used, except for consignments mentioned in point iii above. Isolates recovered in 2021 and 2022 were subjected to antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) and reported to EFSA. Consignments sampled are identified in TRACES as being sampled and all results are marked as satisfactory (no further action required for monitoring results). 6 Conclusions on sampling

However, the gap in the system to detect eligible consignments results in some meat origins and potentially some consignments not being identified at BCPs, which affects the representativeness of sampling at this level.
